results.desc: A nurse, 41, on her third year of double shifts. Not in conflict with anyone, just exhausted and numb. She prays less than she used to.

answers.wanted: Fine, I just barely see them. I'm always at work.
I'm too tired to reach for Him. I haven't turned away, I just have nothing left at the end of a shift.

friction.note: "I've drifted from Him" sounds like it's her fault or her choice. For someone worn out, praying less is about having no energy, not turning away. Neither "drifted" nor "Just there, in the background" quite says it. An option like "I don't have the energy to reach for Him" would fit.
No option says "Relentless" or "It never lets up". "Hard, but I'm getting by" works, but it misses how long this has gone on: three years with no end in sight.
"About the same" undersells "it's been this way for years". An option like "Same as it's been for a long time" would feel more seen.
"A real gift" is a bit sentimental next to the plain options. The list also assumes people are around; there's no "I barely see anyone outside work".
"Worn out" here and "I'm so tired." under the last question overlap. That's fine, but she may wonder if she's repeating herself.

results.overall: She got through it quickly and felt mostly seen: "Worn out", "Numb" and "I'm so tired." all fit her exactly. The God question gave her a small twinge of guilt, because the only honest-ish option framed her praying less as drifting rather than exhaustion.

verdict.why: "Worn down until you feel empty and listless" is exactly my third year of double shifts. I'm not grieving and I'm not in a fight with anyone. I'm just used up. And 102:4, "I even forget to eat my bread", is literally me at 3am on a ward. That verse would make me stop scrolling. The turn at 102:17, that He won't despise the prayer of the destitute, gently answers the guilt I feel about praying less. It says my thin, tired prayers still count. Line 2 is also partly me, because God has slipped into the background. But it asks me to rouse myself, and I don't have the energy for that. So line 1 is the right first match. The wording is a little off in one spot: "you need comfort" assumes I'm reaching for comfort, and honestly I'm numb and not reaching for much. It's still close enough that I'd tap yes.
verdict.wouldHurt: Psalm 102 is printed in full, and in the middle it says "because of Your indignation and Your wrath, for You have lifted me up and cast me down" (102:10). There's also "my enemies reproach me all day" (102:8). For a tired nurse who already feels guilty for praying less, reading that verse with no note could suggest her burnout is God punishing her. The enemies verse doesn't fit someone who isn't in conflict, so she'd feel slightly misread. A short line explaining that these are the psalmist's own words in his distress, not a diagnosis of her, would stop that sting. The "need comfort" framing is also a bit off for someone who feels numb rather than someone asking for comfort.
verdict.theirSituation: Chronic burnout and numbness from years of overwork, with prayer fading from exhaustion rather than doubt or conflict. She's too tired to be reaching for comfort at all.

results.desc: A man, 35, who had an affair. His wife found out last week. He is ashamed and wants to make it right.

answers.wanted: Something I did just came out. 'Something hard just happened' makes it sound like it happened to me, when I caused it.
Both 'Something I've done' and 'Someone I love' (my wife). It's one thing: what I did to her. Being made to pick one felt like splitting it in two.
Something like 'I let Him down', between 'Displeased with me' and 'I've drifted from Him'. The drifting came first, and the affair came out of it.

friction.note: All the 'hard' options are things that happen to you. Someone who caused the crisis has no option that owns it. He might feel the quiz is letting him play the victim.

There's only one pick. When the harm is to someone he loves, 'Something I've done' and 'Someone I love' are the same thing, so choosing one feels like leaving out half of it. Allowing one or two picks, as on the feelings question, would fix it.

'Which is closest?' has no subject, so on a phone he has to guess what it's asking about. Something like 'What's weighing on you most?' would be clearer. None of the options is about wanting to repair the harm or make it right, which is his main thought, as opposed to the sin itself.
There's no option for asking God to help fix the relationship, like 'Help me make it right.' 'Sorry' fits, but it's only half of what he'd say.
'Hard to be around' is ambiguous: are they hard to be around, or is he? 'Upset with me, and with reason' is well worded, and it was a relief to see it.

results.overall: It was quick, and 'Ashamed', 'Upset with me, and with reason' and 'I'm sorry' made him feel seen, not judged. But the options kept treating the crisis as something that happened to him. None of them spoke to his real goal, which is to make it right with his wife.

verdict.why: The first line describes me exactly: I did wrong, I know it, I'm ashamed, and I want to come back. Psalm 51 is the right result. It is the psalm David wrote after his own adultery, so it would feel almost uncomfortably fitting, but it would not feel like an accusation. "Blot out my transgressions" and "wash me, and I will be whiter than snow" give me words I can't find myself, and they hold out hope that I can be clean again. Athanasius's advice is gentle and states my situation plainly, and I'd take that as mercy, not judgment. The line about "a warning from God" would not fit me as well. What I'm feeling is guilt, not dread.
verdict.wouldHurt: Two small risks. First, if the full psalm prints its heading about Nathan coming to David after Bathsheba, it lands very close to home. For most people in my place that heading would say "you are not the first," but for someone raw it could sting. It shouldn't be cut; a quiet line framing it as hope would help. Second, verse 51:4, "Against You, You only, have I sinned," could read as though my wife doesn't count, and making it right with her is half of what I want. The psalm covers only the side of making it right with God. A short note that repentance also means making amends to the people we hurt would keep a man from using the psalm as a way around his wife.

results.desc: A 16-year-old being mocked at school by a group for being a Christian. His parents do not know.

answers.wanted: The kids at school (it's people and school at once, so neither 'People in my life' nor 'Work or school' is quite it)
Close, but it's not stopping it (I believe He's there, that's why they pick on me, but He isn't doing anything about it)
A group of kids at school. 'A whole group of people' and 'People at work or school' both fit and I could only pick one
That it won't stop, and having nobody to tell. 'What they're saying about me' is nearly as true

friction.note: A teenager doesn't think in terms of 'work'. 'Work or school' reads as an adult's option, and 'People in my life' sounds like family and friends, not the kids hassling him. He hesitates between the two.
Single choice, but his real answer is both 'a whole group' and 'at school'. Letting him pick two, or offering 'A group at school or work', would fit.
Putting 'work' first again ('People at work or school') makes it feel like the quiz was written for adults.
'Clear my name.' is an odd thing for a teen being mocked to say, and 'Make me who You want me to be.' sounds a bit like church-camp talk, but neither is pushy. The list is long to scroll on a phone.
Nothing lets him say the secrecy is part of what's hard (his parents don't know). Something like 'Having no one to tell' would fit a lot of teens.
'Near, but quiet' is close, but a kid mocked for his faith may feel sure of God and still let down that nothing changes. 'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' sounds more like doubt than he feels.

results.overall: It went quickly and felt surprisingly personal. The 'Making fun of me' and 'Is your faith part of it?' questions made him feel seen, and 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside' fit him exactly. The only jarring bits were the adult framing around work and not being able to say both 'a group' and 'at school'.

verdict.why: The second half of line 1 is almost word for word what happens to me. Guys at school say "where's your God now?" when something goes wrong for me. So I'd tap yes there. The first half, "long for God with everything in you", is a bit bigger than how I'd put it. I'm not sure I feel that intensely. Mostly I'm just trying not to cave. Still, it's closer than line 2, which is too vague, or line 3, which talks about scheming and fits a group mocking me less well. Psalm 42 would actually land. "Men ask me all day long, Where is your God?" and "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" would make me feel someone had been through this before. The advice not to be troubled and to hope in God is gentle, not preachy. What it misses: it doesn't know I'm dealing with this alone and haven't told my parents. It also doesn't know the mocking comes from a group of people my own age, not "enemies". It speaks to how I feel inside, not to the school situation.
verdict.wouldHurt: "My tears have been my food both day and night" might feel like it's calling me a crybaby, or making this bigger than I'd admit. A teenage boy might back away from that line even when it's true. The word "enemies" in the advice also feels heavy for classmates. Nothing here is wounding, though.
verdict.theirSituation: A teenager keeps quiet at home while a group at school taunts him for his faith. What he needs most is to feel less alone in being mocked for God, and line 1 plus Psalm 42 gives him that.

results.desc: A widow, 72, whose husband of 50 years died four months ago. She is not angry at anyone; she is grieving.

answers.wanted: Something like 'It comes in waves' or 'Still grieving'. Four months on, it isn't worse or better, but 'About the same' sounds flat for grief that rises and falls.
'Grieving' or 'Heartbroken'. 'Sad' feels too small for losing a husband of 50 years. 'Lonely' fits exactly.
'My husband, who died' or 'Someone I've lost'. The option fits, but it groups him with 'something' I've lost.

'Kind, but they've gone back to their own lives'. My children and church were wonderful at first, and now the calls have thinned. 'Gone' was also the nearest way to say the person closest to me has died.
'Near, but I can't feel Him the way I used to'. I haven't lost faith, but He feels quieter since the funeral. Between 'Near, but quiet' and 'Far away'.

friction.note: None of the words names grief or loss, so a new widow has to rate her life 'hard' or 'really hard' as if it were a problem to solve. A 'Grieving' or 'Mourning someone' option would feel seen.
'Something hard just happened' is too sudden for four months, and 'Something hard is finally over' is painful to read, because grief is not over. There is no option for a loss that is ongoing.

'Sad' is labelled 'Sad' but its key is 'heavy'. On screen, 'Sad' reads as too light for bereavement. 'Grieving' is missing from 17 words, which is striking on a quiz that promises a psalm for your situation.
'Someone or something I've lost' puts a dead spouse in the same option as a lost job or house. It is slightly jarring, but acceptable.

'Far away, or gone' is ambiguous. Does 'gone' mean moved away, withdrawn, or dead? A widow may tap it meaning her husband and get read as abandoned. Most of the list is about conflict (against, talking, mocking, upset), which feels off-topic and a little odd to scroll through while grieving.
'Displeased with me' and 'I've drifted from Him' are fine to skip, but no option says 'I trust Him, but it hurts'. A believer in grief is pushed to pick between 'quiet' and 'far'.

'I miss You' could be misread by a widow, who misses her husband, not God. She may pause over it. 'Why?' and 'How long?' could sound like accusing God to someone who says she is not angry. 'Stay with me' fits well.

None of the follow-ups triggered, so the quiz never learns that the loss is a death. That leaves the result to guess from 'Sad, Lonely, Someone I've lost'. A follow-up for focus = loss ('Who or what?' → a death, a marriage, health, a home) would help.

results.overall: It was quick and gentle enough, and 'Stay with me' and 'Lonely' felt right. But no question uses the word grief or death, so she felt she was describing a hard patch rather than mourning her husband. She would wonder whether the psalm she gets really knows what happened.

verdict.why: As a widow four months in, "weighed down, and it won't settle" is true of me: the heaviness comes back every morning. I'd tap yes. "Uneasy" isn't quite my word, because I'm not anxious, I'm bereaved, and nothing in the line admits someone has died. So it reads as a general low mood, not a loss. Psalm 42 still speaks to me. "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" is a question I ask myself. The full psalm has tears "day and night" and "deep calls to deep", which honour the weight without scolding me. It ends on "I will yet praise Him", a hope I can hold without being told to feel better now.
verdict.wouldHurt: Two small things. First, "uneasy" makes deep grief sound like nerves. Second, the advice says "what grieves you is healed". Four months after losing him, that can sound like my grief should already be fixed. Nothing is cruel, but the result never says the word loss.
verdict.theirSituation: She is grieving a husband of 50 years who died four months ago. She is weighed down by sorrow, not anxiety, and she is not angry at anyone.

results.desc: A pastor, 50, whose church board spread a false story about him to the denomination. Two elders he mentored led it.

answers.wanted: Something between 'just happened' and 'getting worse': it happened, and it's still spreading
A few people I trusted turned on me. 'One person' is too few, and 'against me' sounds like everyone
Near, but I can't tell what He's doing about this
People I mentored and led, who are now over me: it's friends, people with power over me and a whole group at once. Wanted to pick two, or 'people at church'
It's happening inside the church, but it isn't about what I believe
Also 'being pushed out'. Would have liked to pick two

friction.note: 'One person has turned on me' is singular. Two elders betraying him falls between that option and 'Against me', and neither names betrayal by people he trusted, which is the heart of it.
Allows only one pick, but a church board is people he trusted, people with power over him and a whole group, all at once. Nothing fits church or ministry. Pastors will be a common audience here.
'Because of what I believe' reads as persecution for faith. His conflict is inside the church but not over belief, so 'Partly' is a guess and could send him to a persecution psalm.
'What they're saying' and 'Being pushed out' are both true for him. It should be pick one or two, like the core questions.
A pastor may not want to admit 'Silent' or 'Far away' even when it's true. The options are fine, but 'Near, but quiet' is an easy place to hide.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly felt right. 'Clear my name.' was exactly what he'd say to God, and that felt almost uncanny. But the follow-ups about who did it made him choose between friends, the people over him and a group, when a betraying church board is all three, and the faith question mixed up church politics with being persecuted for his beliefs.

verdict.why: Line 1 is my situation: the lies came from men I trusted and mentored, others on the board joined in, and I keep replaying it at night. Psalm 55:13 ("my companion and close friend") is the verse I'd have gone looking for myself, and as a pastor I know it well enough that seeing it chosen for me feels right, not like a gimmick. Line 2 (Psalm 26, "vindicate me") would also fit, because I do want the denomination to judge fairly. It would be good if the result mentioned 26 as a companion psalm instead of leaving it as a runner-up I never see.
verdict.wouldHurt: Two small things. "Slander you with idle talk" makes it sound smaller than it is. This was a formal false report to my denomination, and my job is at stake. Also, Psalm 55 goes on to ask for death to take them (55:15). If the "Hard words" note says nothing about that, a hurt man could read it as permission to curse the young men he raised up. A short line saying to hand the verdict to God, not to call down harm, would help. Neither would stop me.
verdict.theirSituation: Men I mentored betrayed me and spread a false report about me to the denomination, and it threatens my ministry.

results.desc: A woman, 29, whose adult sister has cut her off and turned the rest of the family against her.

answers.wanted: It started with one person and now it's spreading. "Getting worse" is close, but it's really one thing that keeps growing.
My family. It's really my sister. "People in my life" sounds too casual, and "Someone or something I've lost" nearly fits too, but she isn't dead. "Family" as its own option would have fit.
"Shutting me out" or "Cut me off". Nobody is exactly making fun of me or openly against me. They've just gone silent and taken her side.
Somewhere between "Far away" and "Just there, in the background". I haven't really been thinking about Him much.

friction.note: The options are all about attack (against me, talking, mocking). Estrangement is mostly silence and being frozen out, and nothing says that. "Far away, or gone" sounds like distance or death, not being cut off on purpose.
"Upset with me, and with reason" felt pointed. I did wonder whether the quiz wanted me to admit it's my fault. Seeing it next to the hurt options made me slightly defensive.
There's no "My family" option, and family is one of the most common things on people's minds. "People in my life" feels vague for something this big.
"Is your faith part of it?" is fine, but it makes the quiz sound like it expects persecution. I answered No quickly and felt the question wasn't about me.
"What they might be planning" sounds paranoid for a family falling-out. "Being pushed out" fit well, though.
Fourteen options is a lot on a phone. There's also nothing like "Bring her back" or "Heal my family". "Help." is generic, so I went with "Why?"

results.overall: It moved fast, and a few answers hit home: hurt and lonely, family, being pushed out. But the people question is written for enemies attacking you, not for a sister who went silent and took the family with her, so I had to translate my situation into attack language. I also wasn't sure whether the result would treat me as the wronged one or as the one at fault.

verdict.why: The first line is close to my life. My own sister turned on me, and she has been turning the rest of the family against me one by one. "Your own people have turned on you" is the part that stops me. It names betrayal from inside the family, not trouble from strangers, and that is exactly the wound. "More and more others are rising up" fits the way relatives drop away one at a time. Psalm 3 turning to "the One who lifts my head" is what I need, because I feel shamed and pushed out. I would say "Yes, that's it" without needing to read the other lines. Line 2, "driven out, on your own," would also be partly true, but it is about the aftermath, not the betrayal.
verdict.wouldHurt: Words like "foes," "rise up against me" and "hounded" make my sister and my family into enemies. I am hurt by them, but I still love them and want them back, so being handed a war psalm about them stings a little. The bigger problem is the full text. Psalm 3:7 ("strike all my enemies on the jaw; break the teeth of the wicked") would feel like I am being asked to pray for harm to my sister and my mother. A short, quiet note under that verse would help a lot, saying the psalmist hands the wrong over to God rather than taking revenge, and that you can pray this while still hoping to be reconciled. Also, "more and more others" is slightly too big for what I am going through: it is my family, not a crowd.
verdict.theirSituation: My sister cut me off and has quietly turned the rest of my family against me; I grieve that loss and want them back, rather than feeling surrounded by enemies.

results.desc: A college student, 20, whose philosophy classmates mock faith. He is starting to doubt, and it scares him.

answers.wanted: Making fun of what I believe. They mock faith in general and it gets to me, but they aren't really picking on me personally.
Classmates. 'People at work or school' is right, but 'work' comes first and it reads like it's meant for adults with jobs.
That their arguments are starting to make sense to me. The hard part isn't what they say about me; it's that I can't answer them and I'm starting to doubt.

friction.note: 'Making fun of me' makes it personal. His classmates mock faith and ideas, not him as a person. There's no option for 'people challenging or mocking what I believe', so he has to overstate it as mockery aimed at him.

Every option assumes enemies who are out to get him: plans, being trapped, being pushed out, not knowing what they'll do next. His hardest part is inside his own head: their arguments are shaking him. 'What they might be planning' and 'Feeling trapped' sound paranoid for a seminar room, and they push him toward a 'surrounded by enemies' result when his real situation is doubt.

Once he taps 'mocking' and 'Yes, it's because of what I believe', the follow-ups read like a persecution track. A doubting student could feel boxed in as a victim when what he wants is help with the question 'is any of this true?'
'I'm not sure He's there' is good and honest. He'd appreciate that it's allowed without sounding like a warning.
'People at work or school' lumps two very different settings together. A student would like 'classmates' or 'people at school' on its own line.

results.overall: Most of it felt quick and oddly understanding: 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside', 'I'm not sure He's there' and 'Are You there?' land well for a scared doubter. But once he said he's being mocked for his faith, the follow-ups turned into a persecution script about enemies and plots, and none of it touched what actually scares him: that the arguments are getting through.

verdict.why: Line 1 misses: I'm not longing for God with everything in me. I'm scared I'm losing Him, and nobody is sobbing at me "Where is your God?". My classmates just argue. Line 2 is what I'd tap. "Close to losing your footing" is exactly how the doubt feels, and admitting it is the scary part. Psalm 73 is someone who nearly let go and ends with "You hold my right hand", which is what I'd want to hear. Line 3 actually describes my setting more literally (the mockery), but I'd stop at 2 first. And honestly, I'd be relieved not to land on Psalm 14. Being told "the fool says there is no God… their acts are vile" about classmates I like, while I half-agree with them, would feel like I'm being called a fool too. The fit is near, not exact. Psalm 73's trigger is envying the prosperous wicked, not intellectual doubt, so the body of the psalm will partly feel like someone else's story. The turn at verse 23 lands, though.
verdict.wouldHurt: The Athanasius advice for Psalm 73 is garbled English: "Sing the Psalms, and whatever in you has slipped comes to admit it". It reads like a broken sentence and makes the whole thing feel machine-made just when I need it to feel trustworthy. Also, nothing names doubt or intellectual challenge directly. The psalm's middle section, about envying rich, arrogant people, doesn't match me, so I might feel the quiz grabbed the closest thing it had. If I had landed on line 3, Psalm 14's opening would feel like it was calling my friends (and me) vile fools.
verdict.theirSituation: A 20-year-old whose faith is being worn down by smart, likeable classmates' arguments. He is afraid he is losing his belief. He doesn't feel persecuted or full of longing.

results.desc: A man, 45, laid off after 20 years. Money is tight and he feels useless. Nobody is against him.

answers.wanted: Something like 'Stuck' or 'Slowly getting worse as the money runs down'. 'About the same' is true but undersells the pressure.
'Useless' or 'Like I'm no good to anyone'. That is the real word; 'Ashamed' was the nearest, and anxious covers the money.
'Losing my job' or 'Being out of work'. Work and money are tied for first; one option joining them would fit.

'Nothing I did, I just feel like a failure' or 'Not being able to provide'. His shame comes from being laid off, not from a sin. Every option here assumes wrongdoing or temptation, so he picked 'Something I did' only because he half blames himself.

friction.note: Tapping 'Ashamed' sends him to a follow-up that only offers sin-shaped answers (something I did, a habit, my thoughts, God warning me). A man ashamed because he lost his job and can't provide is quietly told his shame must be about wrongdoing. That feels like being put in a box and a bit accusatory. It needs a 'not something I did, I just feel I've failed' option, or the follow-up shouldn't fire from 'Ashamed' alone.
There is no 'Useless', 'Worthless' or 'Like a failure', which is the most common feeling after a layoff. 'Ashamed' stands in for it, and that is what sends him down the wrong follow-up.
'Work or school' reads as stress at a job he still has. There is nothing for being out of work, and he has to choose between Work and Money when it is really one thing.
There is no option for 'stuck', or for a slow grind that isn't clearly getting worse. 'About the same' sounds flatter than how it feels.

results.overall: Quick, and mostly easy to answer. The questions about the people around him and God ('Silent. I pray and nothing changes') and 'Help.' landed well. But he had no word for feeling useless, and the shame follow-up treated his job loss like a sin to confess, which would sting a bit on a phone.

verdict.why: Line 1 is not me. I lost my job; I didn't do anything wrong, so I'd tap "Not quite" straight away. Line 2, "weighed down or uneasy, and it won't settle", is honestly how the months since the layoff feel, so I'd say yes. It's vague enough to fit almost anyone, though. It catches the mood but not the actual thing: feeling useless after 20 years, and worrying about money. "Why are you downcast, O my soul? Put your hope in God" would speak to me. It reads like a man talking himself out of a slump, and that's where I am. Most of Psalm 42, though, is about longing for God and remembering worship. It says nothing about work, provision or being needed. Verse 10 has foes taunting "Where is your God?", and nobody is doing that to me. So it helps with the heaviness but leaves the core of my situation untouched. Looking at the fallback, "It's grinding me down" (Psalm 102, days vanishing like smoke, withered like grass) might actually fit my feeling of uselessness better than 42 does.
verdict.wouldHurt: Line 1 comes up first as my "best match": "You've done wrong, you know it, you're ashamed." For a man who already feels like a failure after a layoff, that quietly suggests losing the job was his own fault, and it could sting. Psalm 42's lines about enemies taunting also don't fit someone with nobody against him. That's only a small mismatch, not a wound.
verdict.theirSituation: He's grieving the loss of his work and his sense of being useful, and he's anxious about money. He isn't guilty of anything and nobody is against him, so a line about a restless, weighed-down soul fits the mood but not the cause.

results.desc: A woman, 33, anxious all the time for no reason she can name. She lies awake at night.

answers.wanted: I can't tell what it is, it's just there all the time
I don't know, I can't feel much of anything when I'm this wound up
Let me rest / Give me peace / Quiet my mind

friction.note: "Nothing in particular" sounds like nothing is wrong. For someone anxious with no clear cause it reads as brushing her off. "I can't put my finger on it" would fit her better and still means the same thing.
Nothing covers not sleeping or lying awake, which is the most concrete thing in her life right now. She picks "Worn out" as the closest. A "Can't switch off" or "On edge" option would catch her.

None of the fourteen lines asks for rest or calm, which is what an anxious person lying awake would say first. "Help." works but is generic. The list leans toward complaint and praise, and a plain "Give me peace" is missing.
The options assume she knows how God feels to her. When anxiety drowns everything out, she may just not know. "Far away" is the nearest, but it adds a sadness she didn't choose.
"About the same" fits, but after "Fine on the outside, not on the inside" it feels a bit flat for something that has been going on a long time. "It's been like this a while" would say it better.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and mostly easy, and \"Fine on the outside, not on the inside\" felt like it was written for her. But anxiety with no cause, and lying awake, had no clear home in the options, so she ended up answering near her situation instead of about it.

verdict.why: Line 1 misreads me. I'm not empty or listless. I'm keyed up, and I'm tired only because I can't sleep. Line 2's "uneasy, and it won't settle" is the closest words anyone has put to it, so I'd tap yes there. Psalm 42's "Why the unease within me?" asks the question I can't answer myself. It doesn't demand a reason for the anxiety, and it turns to hope without telling me to stop feeling it. That lands. What's missing is the night. Nothing notices that I lie awake, and a psalm like 4 ("I will lie down and sleep in peace") would have felt made for me. "Weighed down" also tilts toward sadness, and mine is more of a hum of dread than a weight.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. The "weighed down" half of line 2 and the downcast, tearful tone of Psalm 42 lean toward depression, so I might feel slightly filed under the wrong thing. It's not enough to put me off.
verdict.theirSituation: She has constant anxiety she can't explain and lies awake at night. She's restless and on edge rather than sad or empty, and no line speaks to the sleeplessness or the night.

results.desc: A new believer, 24, baptised a month ago, full of joy, seeing God everywhere.

answers.wanted: Mostly kind, but a couple of old friends don't get the new me: something like 'Kind, though some don't get my faith'
Both 'Thank You.' and 'How great You are.' together; having to choose just one felt like splitting one feeling in two

friction.note: This is one pick only, while 'feel' and 'people' allow two. For a joyful person, 'Thank You', 'How great You are' and 'Make me who You want me to be' are all true at once, so choosing just one felt arbitrary. Two picks would help here too.
'Clear my name.' and 'It isn't fair.' come across as odd or heavy to someone in a happy season. That's fine, because there are plenty of options, but the list is long (14) to scroll on a phone.

Six of the nine options are negative or distant. A happy new believer reads past a lot of struggle before reaching 'Close' and 'Clearly at work'. It doesn't push toward an answer, but the question leans toward trouble.

There's nothing for mixed reactions to a new faith: some people kind, some puzzled or distant, but not 'against me' or 'making fun of me'. A new believer has probably met this, and 'Talking about me' is too strong.
The key for 'Sad' is 'heavy', which the person never sees. Otherwise the list is fine. 'Grateful' and 'Happy' next to each other made it easy.
'Coming to faith, mine or someone else's' fitted perfectly and felt like the quiz had noticed me. No complaints.

results.overall: Quick and easy, and it felt warm. The follow-up about what's behind the good landed exactly on 'coming to faith', which felt personal. The only snags were picking just one thing to say to God when thanks and praise felt like the same breath, and a people question with no room for friends who are puzzled by the new faith.

verdict.why: Full of joy and seeing God everywhere, I'd honestly tap yes on "You just want to sing to God", and Psalm 93 ("The LORD reigns! He is robed in majesty") matches how big God feels to me right now. The second line would have fit me even better. It names being made new, maybe myself, and being amazed at God's love. That is exactly my first month after baptism, and Psalm 32's "Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven" would have made me cry. Line 1 is true but general. Line 2 is my story. Since the order puts the general line first, I'd stop there and never see the result that fits better. Ranking this line second for a newly baptised person is a missed chance, not a misreading. The word "just" in "just want to sing" also shrinks the feeling a little, as if my joy had no reason behind it.
verdict.theirSituation: I was baptised a month ago and I'm overflowing with joy. It's joy about being made new, not only a general urge to praise, so the baptism line (Psalm 32) is more precisely me than the singing line.

results.desc: A mother, 38, whose son has a serious illness. She is afraid and praying constantly.

answers.wanted: Nothing has changed yet, and we're waiting on the doctors. It feels like it's getting worse, but I don't want to say that.
I'm holding on to Him with everything. He feels like all I have, but He hasn't answered yet.
Please heal him.

friction.note: Every option is about me and God. There is no prayer for someone else, like 'Heal him' or 'Save my child', and that is the one thing she is praying all day. 'Help.' is the nearest, but it feels like a stand-in.

Nothing fits praying constantly and clinging to God while He seems not to answer. 'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' sounds like complaint or lost faith, and 'Close' ignores how frightened she is. She might feel pushed into sounding faithless.

Tapping 'Getting worse' about a sick child's condition feels like saying it out loud, and some mothers will flinch at that. There is no 'Waiting to find out' or 'Up in the air' option, and that is where many families with a serious diagnosis are.

Coming right after she has told the quiz someone she loves is ill, a question about whether people are against her or talking about her feels off-topic. It's harmless, but it reminds her this is a general form.
'I'm losing them' is right next to 'They're ill, or in danger', and a frightened mother may be unsure which one she is allowed to pick. Seeing 'losing them' as an option can hurt.

results.overall: Mostly quick and gentle, and 'Someone I love' then 'They're ill, or in danger' made her feel seen. The questions about God and what she would say to Him felt built for someone praying about themselves, not for a mother pleading for her son.

verdict.why: Line 1 misses me. I'm not empty or listless. I'm on high alert, praying all day and night. "Life has worn you down" also sounds like general tiredness, and this is my son. Line 2 is what's going on: I'm afraid, and I need something to hold on to. So I'd tap "Yes, that's it" there. Psalm 118:14 ("The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation") is something I would hold on to. Athanasius's line that the part of me that is afraid "is strengthened by hope" speaks to me directly. Two things only partly fit. The quiz never sees that my fear is for someone else, not me. And the psalm's first line ("What can man do to me?") is about human enemies, but my enemy is a disease. Line 3 (pleading, needing words to pray) would also have fit me, because I am praying constantly. Psalm 5 is about enemies and the wicked, though, so 118 is the better of the two for me.
verdict.wouldHurt: Printed in full, Psalm 118 is a victory song: "I will not die, but I will live" (118:17), "This is the day the LORD has made; we will rejoice" (118:24). When my son's outcome is unknown, 118:17 could read as a promise that might not be kept, or feel like a knife if things go badly. The joyful thanksgiving can feel like it skips ahead of where I am. A short note framing it as hope to hold on to, not a promise about the outcome, would help. Showing the "worn down, empty" line first also slightly misreads a frightened mother as a burned-out one. That's not hurtful, just off.
verdict.theirSituation: She is frightened for her seriously ill son and praying all the time; the fear is for him, not for herself, and she is anxious and alert rather than emptied out.

results.desc: A man, 55, whose business rival cheated his way to success while he stayed honest and struggled. He is bitter and envious.

answers.wanted: One man who cheated and got ahead of me. That's people and work together, and neither option says it.
Most people are fine. One competitor cheated and got rich while I stayed honest. He isn't 'turning on me' or 'against me', he just beat me dirty.
I did it the right way and He let the cheat win. Not far off or silent exactly, more like 'not rewarding the honest one'.

friction.note: All the negative options (against me, turned on me, talking about me, mocking me) are about being attacked. A rival who cheated to get ahead isn't attacking him, so he's forced to tap 'Fine' even though another person is the whole problem. The list is missing something like 'Someone got ahead of me unfairly' or 'Doing better than me, and they don't deserve it'.
There's no 'someone else's success' or 'a rival'. 'People in my life' sounds like family and friends, and 'Work' leaves out the cheating. He'd pause before tapping.

Nothing says 'Envious' or 'Jealous'. He might not admit to those words anyway, and 'Bitter' carries him. But if the result is Psalm 73 or 37, the quiz has no way to know the envy is there, except through 'Bitter' combined with 'Bad people doing well'.

'What gets to you most?' about 'the way the world is' is broader than his complaint, which is personal: one man. 'Bad people doing well' fits well, but he only reached this question through 'It isn't fair'. If he'd tapped 'Why?' instead, he'd never see the one option that describes him.

'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' is close, but a man like this may not be praying much. There's no option like 'I did right and He let the wrong man win'. The options assume a devotional life this bitter man may not have.

results.overall: Quick and mostly painless, and 'It isn't fair' plus 'Bad people doing well' felt like it finally understood him. But the people and focus questions have no place for 'a cheat beat me', so he had to tap 'Fine' and 'Work' while thinking 'that's not it'. Whether he gets the right result depends on him happening to pick 'It isn't fair'.

verdict.why: This is my situation almost word for word. A cheat is doing well and I stayed honest and I'm struggling, and yes, it's shaking me. Then 73:3 says "I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked," which is exactly the thing I'm ashamed of and wouldn't have said out loud. It's the psalmist saying it about himself, not the quiz accusing me, so I feel seen instead of scolded. The turn at 73:17, "then I discerned their end," gives me something to do with the bitterness besides chew on it. The line is slightly general: it says "people who don't care about God," while my rival is one man who lied and cheated. It's close enough that I'd tap yes right away.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. The one small risk is that "they end badly" could feed a wish for revenge in a bitter reader. Psalm 3's standard of writing out what the psalm does (the psalmist admits his own envy and folly in 73:21-22) would guard against that.
verdict.theirSituation: One particular rival got ahead by cheating while I stayed honest and struggled, and I'm eaten up with envy and bitterness about it.

results.desc: Denise, 52, Ohio, United Methodist. Her mother has dementia and moved in with her family in the spring; last Sunday her mother didn't know who she was. She is worn out, snaps at her husband over small things, and when she prays it feels like talking to the ceiling.

answers.wanted: They've been patient with me. I'm the one who's been hard to be around, snapping at my husband.

friction.note: Every option is about how others treat me. There is nothing for 'they've been fine, it's me who's short with them', so her guilt about snapping has nowhere to go. 'Hard to be around' is the nearest, but tapping it would feel like blaming her mother, who can't help it. 'Upset with me, and with reason' overstates it.

'I'm losing them' fits, but it reads like death. What she's living is a slow loss while she does the caring: her mother is still here but doesn't know her. There's no option for 'I'm caring for them and it's wearing me down', and that load is half of what she's going through.

'Getting worse' and 'Something hard just happened' both fit, because the day her mother didn't know her was a sudden blow inside a slow decline. You can only pick one, so she'd hesitate here for a moment.
'Someone I love' and 'Someone or something I've lost' overlap for anyone watching dementia. Fine to pick one, but it's a small fork.

results.overall: It was quick and felt kind. The God and 'say' questions put her feelings ('talking to the ceiling', 'I'm so tired') into words better than she could. The one place she felt boxed in was the people question: none of the options let her admit she's the one who's been short-tempered, and nothing names the everyday weight of caregiving.

verdict.why: "Worn down until you feel empty... and you need comfort" is Denise's life right now: months of caregiving, running on nothing. Psalm 102 speaks to her directly. "Withered like grass; I even forget to eat my bread" is exactly what a caregiver's day feels like. And the turn, "He will not despise their prayer," answers her real fear, that prayer is just talking to the ceiling. She would feel seen and would say yes on the first line. Line 2 (Psalm 42) is also close and would be a fine second choice, but "won't settle" sounds more like anxiety than the exhaustion she actually has.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Listless" only half fits. She isn't flat, she's frayed and snapping at her husband, so that part of the line doesn't match her. The printed psalm includes 102:10 ("because of Your indignation and Your wrath, You have lifted me up and cast me away"). A tired, guilty caregiver could read that as her mother's illness being God's anger at her. It needs a gentle word nearby or it could sting. Nothing names the grief of her mother not knowing her, but the honest fallback wording covers that gap without pretending.
verdict.theirSituation: A worn-out caregiver whose mother with dementia no longer recognises her. She is grieving someone still alive, feels guilty about being short-tempered, and her prayers feel unheard.

results.desc: Kwame, 34, Accra, Ghana, Pentecostal. A coworker told their manager that Kwame had been taking money from petty cash, and there is now an investigation even though he did nothing. He is angry and scared of losing the job, and his wife keeps telling him to pray while he mostly lies awake rehearsing what he'll say.

answers.wanted: Being accused of something I didn't do. It's work, but really it's the lie and the investigation.
I know He's there, I just can't settle to pray. My wife keeps telling me to, and I lie awake going over what I'll say instead.
That it's a lie and I could lose my job over it. Waiting for the investigation to decide.

friction.note: No option for a false accusation or trouble at work caused by someone else. 'Work or school' sounds like workload, and 'People in my life' sounds like family. I had to pick one half of it.

Every option is about what 'they' say or plan. There's nothing for waiting on a decision from someone in authority, like an investigation or a manager's verdict, and that's the part keeping him up at night. 'Being pushed out' comes close but sounds like office politics, not being accused of theft.

A Pentecostal man would not tap 'I'm not sure He's there' or 'I've drifted'. What's really true is 'I believe, but I'm too angry and worried to pray', and there's no option for that. 'Just there, in the background' feels like a slight admission of guilt.
'Upset with me, and with reason' sits right next to the accusation options. For someone falsely accused, it reads like the quiz is quietly asking whether he actually did it.

results.overall: It was quick, and 'Clear my name.' felt like the quiz had understood his exact situation, which was a relief. The middle questions (focus, the hardest part, God) kept making him squeeze a false accusation and an anxious wait into boxes built for workload or general conflict.

verdict.why: I'd say "Yes, that's it" to the first line. I have been falsely accused and I want someone to finally judge who is right. That is exactly what keeps me up at night. Psalm 26 opens "Vindicate me, O LORD! For I have walked with integrity", and that is the prayer I have been failing to put into words while I rehearse my defence. My wife keeps telling me to pray, and this gives me words to pray with. Athanasius tells me to ask God to be the Judge and not to let a human verdict have the last word. That speaks straight to the lying awake. The turn at 26:12, "my feet stand on level ground", gives me something to stand on. It is not exact, though. "They won't stop trying to ruin you" sounds like a long campaign by many enemies. Mine is one coworker and one accusation, now under investigation. Line 1 also misses how afraid I am of losing the job. Line 2 (Psalm 118) would have caught that half too.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. On a bad night, "don't let any human verdict be the last word" could sound like it brushes off my real fear about the investigation and my family's income. The psalm speaks to my innocence but not to my fear of losing the job.
verdict.theirSituation: One coworker has falsely accused me of theft. There is an investigation at work, and I am angry, afraid for my job and not sleeping. What I want is to be proved innocent, not a way to survive a long run of attacks.

results.desc: Rachel, 38, Manchester, UK, Church of England. Their third round of IVF failed last month, and two friends have announced pregnancies since. She has stopped going to the family service and isn't sure God is listening, though she hasn't said that out loud to anyone.

answers.wanted: Something hard happened, and it keeps getting rubbed in (every new pregnancy announcement)
Grieving, or Empty. 'Sad' is too small for it, and she's not sure she wants to own 'Bitter' but it's true
Something I've been hoping and waiting for, e.g. 'A child', or 'Something I want and can't have'
Happy about things that hurt me (they've done nothing wrong, it's just painful to be around them)

friction.note: There's no option for longing or waiting for something that hasn't come: infertility, singleness, a prayer that hasn't been answered. 'Someone or something I've lost' is the nearest, but calling a baby she never had 'lost' feels wrong to her and a bit raw. 'Someone I love' doesn't fit either.

There's no word for grief. 'Sad' feels too light for it. 'Bitter' is honest, but tapping it feels like admitting to something shameful, so some people in her position will pick 'Hurt' or 'Worn out' instead.

There's nothing for people who are kind and doing nothing wrong but whose good news still hurts. 'Hard to be around' is close, but it quietly blames them. Most of the options are about hostility, which doesn't match her situation.
'Something hard just happened' and 'Getting worse' are both partly true here. It's a one-off blow followed by reminders that keep coming, so she has to pick one half of it.
'Why?', 'It isn't fair.', 'How long?' and 'Are You there?' all fit, and she can only pick one. She'd want to pick two, the way the feelings question allows.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and mostly gentle. 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside' and 'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' felt like they'd read her mind. But none of the questions has a place for the grief of longing for something that never came, so she was pushed onto 'loss' and 'Sad', and she'll wonder whether the psalm she gets really fits her.

verdict.why: As Rachel I would tap "Yes, that's it" on the first line. It is soft enough to say yes to without admitting anything, and "it won't settle" is exactly how the last month has felt. The line itself is generic, though. It names a mood, not the grief, and not the private fear that God isn't listening. So I'd feel roughly understood rather than truly seen. Psalm 42 turns out to be a much better match than the line suggests. 42:3 ("my tears have been my food day and night, while they say to me all day long, 'Where is your God?'") and 42:9 ("Why have You forgotten me?") put into words the thing I haven't said out loud. 42:4 remembers going to the house of God with the crowd, and it would hit hard given that I've stopped going to the family service. That is where I'd feel seen. But the preview shows only the two refrain verses (42:5 and 42:11), which both end in "Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him". Shown alone, they read like the tidy answer a well-meaning friend gives, and that isn't the psalm's real honesty. Since the full psalm is printed, the lament will be there. The card and the turn should lead with the lament verses, not the hopeful resolution. Athanasius's line "what grieves you is healed" also feels too quick for someone a month past a failed third IVF round.
verdict.wouldHurt: Leading with "Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him" twice, with nothing about the tears or the "where is your God?" taunts beside it, could read as being told to cheer up and trust more. For someone quietly doubting that God listens, that pressure pushes her away. "What grieves you is healed" promises healing too early. And if the 988 crisis line appears on a hard path, it is a US number that is useless in Manchester; a UK visitor needs Samaritans (116 123) or a line for her location.
verdict.theirSituation: She is grieving a failed third round of IVF, stung by friends' pregnancy news, has quietly pulled away from church, and privately fears God isn't listening, so this is grief plus hidden doubt, not just unease.

results.desc: Tom, 44, Houston, Texas, non-denominational church. He started drinking again after fourteen months sober and hasn't told his sponsor or his wife. He feels deeply ashamed and half believes God has run out of patience with him.

answers.wanted: They don't know. My wife is being kind, but only because I haven't told her.
Done with me. Out of patience with me.
I'm sorry, and help, both. Something like: Don't give up on me.

friction.note: None of the options covers 'they don't know what's going on with me'. For someone hiding a relapse, 'Fine' and 'Kind to me' are true on the surface but miss the point, and picking 'Kind' stings because he knows he's deceiving them. 'Upset with me, and with reason' is what he's afraid of, but it hasn't happened yet.

'Displeased with me' is too mild for what he's afraid of. He thinks God may have run out of patience with him, and there's no option like 'Done with me' or 'Tired of me'. 'I've drifted from Him' doesn't fit either, because he didn't drift; he fell back.
He'd want to tap both 'I'm sorry' and 'Help.' but only one is allowed. Pick-one works less well here than it does for the feelings question.
'Something I keep going back to' fits well, and it names the relapse without saying it. 'A sense that God is warning me' could feel ominous to someone who already fears God is fed up with him.

results.overall: Quick, and it felt surprisingly personal: 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside' and 'Something I keep going back to' landed hard for Tom. The weak spots were having no way to say the people around him don't know, and no God option strong enough for 'He's run out of patience with me.'

verdict.why: Line 1 names Tom's night almost word for word: he did wrong, he knows it, and he is ashamed. "Want to come back" is the part he would hesitate over, because he half believes the door is shut. He would still tap yes, because wanting to come back is exactly why the shame hurts. Psalm 51:1 answers his real fear. It appeals to God's "loving devotion" and "great compassion", which is the opposite of a God who has run out of patience. 51:7, "wash me, and I will be whiter than snow", gives him the hope that he can be clean again, and he would reread it. Many people in 12-step recovery already know Psalm 51 as the relapse psalm, so it would feel right to him, not forced. Line 2 (warning, shaking) is partly true but about fear, not guilt. Line 3 is too vague for someone who knows exactly what he did.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing would wound him. One small misread is Athanasius's line "you are turning back, and you are asking for mercy". Tom has not turned back yet: he is still hiding the drinking from his sponsor and his wife. The line credits him with a step he hasn't taken. That could feel like a gentle push, or it could leave him feeling like a fraud, as if the psalm is for people who have already confessed. Adding "or wanting to" to that line would close the gap. The quiz says nothing about telling the people in his life, and that is right, since it isn't the quiz's place. But a quiet line under the result saying that Psalm 51 is often prayed before a hard conversation would meet him where he actually is.
verdict.theirSituation: A man who relapsed after 14 months sober, is hiding it from his sponsor and wife, is ashamed, and fears God's patience with him is used up.

results.desc: Maria, 29, Mexico City, Catholic. Her husband left her for someone at his work, and the divorce is being finalised while she and her four-year-old live with her parents. She still goes to Mass but usually cries through it, and she feels embarrassed in front of people who were at the wedding.

answers.wanted: Something is ending and I'm in the middle of it (the divorce is being finalised right now)
Hurt, Sad and Ashamed all at once. Two isn't enough, but hurt and ashamed are the truest
One person betrayed me / left me, and my family is kind to me
I still go to Him, but I just cry. Somewhere between far away and near but quiet
My husband (a spouse or partner)
That he chose someone else over me / the betrayal itself, and facing people who were at our wedding
Nothing I did. I'm ashamed of what happened to me, of being left

friction.note: I only got this question because I picked 'Ashamed', and every option assumes my shame is guilt: something I did, a habit, my thoughts, God warning me. I'm embarrassed because I was left. That's not a sin. Being forced to pick one of these felt like the quiz was blaming me for my husband leaving. 'A sense that God is warning me' would really sting at this point. It needs an option like 'Nothing I did. It's what was done to me', or ashamed shouldn't trigger this question at all.
'One person has turned on me' sounds like a fight or a feud. A husband leaving for someone else is betrayal and abandonment. There's no option for 'someone I trusted left me' or 'betrayed me'.

This whole list is about enemies scheming (planning, what they'll do next, it keeps growing). It's written for being persecuted, not for being abandoned. 'Being pushed out' was the nearest option, but it doesn't fit.
There's no spouse or partner option. Lumping my husband in with 'family, or the people closest to me' works technically, but it feels off.
There's no option for 'a painful thing is in the middle of ending'. 'Getting worse' and 'Something hard just happened' both miss the fact that it's slow and ongoing.
Only one or two words is tight when hurt, sad and ashamed are all true at once, but I could live with it.
Nothing covers 'I keep showing up to Him, but I just cry'. It's closer to 'near, but I'm too hurt to feel it' than to 'far away'.

results.overall: Most of the questions were quick and felt kind, and 'Someone or something I've lost' and 'Why?' were exactly right. But because I'm divorcing, the enemy-themed follow-ups didn't fit me, and the shame question treated my embarrassment as if it were my own sin. That part hurt and made me wary of the result.

verdict.why: Line 1 almost reaches her, since her husband did turn on her, but the rest doesn't fit. Nobody is "rising up against" her and she has no growing crowd of foes. What she feels is shame in front of wedding guests, not attack, so she would say "Not quite." Line 2 is simply true: she is weighed down and it won't settle. Psalm 42 then speaks to her more than the line promised. It has "my tears have been my food day and night", remembering going "with the throng to the house of God", and people asking "Where is your God?". For a woman who cries through Mass and feels watched by people who knew her married, that would land hard and gently. The turn to "put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him" gives her somewhere to go without telling her to cheer up.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing in Psalm 42 would wound her. The only friction is that the line she says yes to is general. It names the heaviness but not the betrayal or the shame of being left, so she may feel the quiz caught her mood but not her story. Line 1, shown first, casts her situation as enemies multiplying against her, which could feel slightly off or dramatic. Nothing she sees acknowledges that she has been abandoned.
verdict.theirSituation: She was abandoned and betrayed by her husband, and she is grieving and ashamed in front of her own community, including at Mass. She is sad and humiliated rather than under attack.

results.desc: Annamma, 61, Kerala, India, Syro-Malabar Catholic. Her husband died four months ago, and the visits and phone calls have mostly stopped. The house is very quiet in the evenings, and she talks to God the way she used to talk to him, not sure anyone answers.

answers.wanted: Quieter than before: the first weeks were full of people and now it is empty
They came at first, but now they have gone back to their own lives
I talk to Him, but I don't hear anything back (I'm not asking for anything to change)

friction.note: She taps 'Someone or something I've lost' and nothing more is asked. There is no follow-up for grief, but 'Someone I love' gets its own. A widow expects the next question to ask who she lost, and when none comes it feels like the quiz skipped past her.

'Far away, or gone' is unclear for someone who has lost a person. 'Gone' can read as dead, which would be her husband, not the neighbours and relatives who stopped calling. Something like 'Not around like they used to be' would fit her without that sting.
There is no option for 'they were there at first, then drifted off'. The pullback after a funeral is a very common experience.

'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' assumes she is asking God for something that is not happening. Her prayer is conversation, not petition, and nothing can change her loss. The words 'nothing changes' feel a little bitter for a devout Catholic. 'I'm not sure He's there' is too strong for her, so she is caught between the two.
'About the same' does not capture a grief that has gone quiet rather than better or worse. An option like 'Quieter, emptier' would fit.
'Really hard' and 'Hard, but I'm getting by' are fine, but she might hesitate, because saying 'really hard' feels like complaining. Not a real problem.

results.overall: Quick and gentle, and 'Lonely', 'Sad' and 'Stay with me.' fitted her exactly. But the quiz never asks about her loss after she names it, and the people and God options assume conflict or petition rather than the quiet absence of widowhood, so she would feel only half-seen going into her result.

verdict.why: I would tap yes. It is not exactly my life. I am not "uneasy", I am grieving, and "it won't settle" makes it sound like nerves or worry. But "weighed down, and it won't settle" is close enough to the heaviness of the evenings, and nothing else on offer is closer. Psalm 42 turns out to be almost uncannily right: tears as food day and night, "where is your God?", pouring out my soul as I remember walking with the crowd to God's house. That is how I talk to God now without knowing if He answers, and how I remember the busy house before it went quiet. "Deep calls to deep" would stay with me. The psalm does more than the line that led to it.
verdict.wouldHurt: It hurts a little that the word grief never appears. "Uneasy" and "won't settle" make a widow's sorrow sound like anxiety or a mood. Also, if the only verse I see on the card is "Why are you downcast... Put your hope in God", it can read like a gentle telling-off to cheer up and have more faith. The full psalm, with the tears and the waves, is what keeps it from sounding that way, so it should be shown before or alongside that verse. The advice "what grieves you is healed" helps, but four months in, "healed" could sound as if I am meant to be further along than I am.
verdict.theirSituation: A recent widow grieving in a house that has gone quiet, still talking to God and unsure He answers. Hers is grief and loneliness, not unease.

results.desc: Daniel, 19, Nairobi, Kenya, Anglican. He didn't get the grades for the university course his parents had been counting on, and his cousins all did. He feels like a disappointment and doubts God pays attention to something as small as exam results.

answers.wanted: My exam results, and what happens to my plans now (torn between 'Work or school' and 'What's next for me')
Disappointed in me (my parents), and my cousins just make me feel small, even though they aren't doing anything wrong
Like He doesn't bother with something as small as my exam results
I didn't do well enough and let my family down. It's a failure, not a wrong I did

friction.note: 'Upset with me, and with reason' is the only option for family disappointment, and 'and with reason' makes him agree he deserves it. He'd want a plain 'Disappointed in me'. Nothing covers people who are doing nothing wrong but make you feel small by comparison, like cousins who all passed.
No option for 'He's there, but this is too small for Him to care about'. That is his actual doubt. 'Far away' and 'I'm not sure He's there' both miss it.

This follow-up was triggered by 'Ashamed' and 'Upset with me', but every option points to sin or habit ('Something I keep going back to', 'Where my thoughts have taken me', 'A sense that God is warning me'). Failing an exam is not a moral failing, so it feels like the quiz is pushing him to treat disappointment as guilt. He'd want an option like 'I let people down' or 'I didn't measure up'.
'Work or school' and 'What's next for me' both fit about equally. He might wish he could pick two here.

results.overall: The questions were quick and mostly felt like they were about him. But the quiz kept reading his shame as guilt: once he tapped 'Ashamed', the follow-ups assumed he had done something wrong, when what he actually feels is 'I failed and disappointed my family, and God probably doesn't care about exams.'

verdict.why: Line 1 isn't me. Failing my exams wasn't a sin, and I have nothing to repent of, so I'd tap "Not quite". Line 2 fits: I'm downcast, the feeling won't settle, and "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" is what I keep asking myself. Psalm 42 also asks God "why have You forgotten me?", which is my real doubt: does He even notice something as small as exam results? "Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him" meets me there without making the exams sound silly.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing in the Psalm 42 result would hurt. But being offered the shame-and-repentance line first stings a little. It suggests the quiz read my disappointing my parents as a sin to confess, which feeds the shame I already carry. Neither line names my real situation (letting my family down, cousins who did better, doubting God cares about small things), so it feels close but not exact.
verdict.theirSituation: He failed to get the grades his family was counting on while his cousins succeeded, so he feels like a disappointment and wonders whether God pays attention to something this small.

results.desc: Grace, 47, Seoul, South Korea, Presbyterian. Her lupus has flared badly for two months and she has had to cut back her hours at work. She is tired of being tired and a little tired of people telling her they are praying for her healing.

answers.wanted: It's dragging on / a flare that won't let up. It's chronic, so 'about the same' sounds too calm, and 'getting worse' isn't quite true either
Worn out, plus 'Fed up' or 'Frustrated'. Angry and Bitter are too strong for her
Kind, but they keep saying the wrong thing (the 'praying for your healing' line). 'Hard to be around' is too harsh for people who mean well
There, but I'm too tired to feel Him. 'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' was close, but it sounds like an accusation she wouldn't make

friction.note: None of the options fits a chronic illness that flares and settles. 'About the same' plays it down, and 'Something hard is finally over' will never apply. Something like 'Dragging on' would help anyone with a long illness
There's no word for mild frustration or being fed up. The only choices are Angry and Bitter, which feel too strong to admit to, so she plays it safe with Worn out alone
There's no way to say 'kind but draining'. The main irritant in her life is well-meant spiritual comments, and every option makes her call people either good or bad
'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' puts two claims in one option. She may pray without expecting a cure, so the second half reads as though healing is the measure of whether God is present
Fine. 'I'm so tired.' is exactly what she'd say, and she was glad to see it
She would be put off if the psalm or the note under it promised healing, or read like one more 'I'm praying for your healing'. She wants to be met in endurance, not given a cure narrative

results.overall: It was quick, and most of it felt kind and plain. 'I'm so tired.' and 'My health' fit her exactly. The questions assume a hard time either ends or changes, though, so a chronic flare only half fits, and she had no way to say people are kind but wearing.

verdict.why: "Worn down until you feel empty and listless" is exactly "tired of being tired". It names what the lupus is doing to me without making the quiz about my disease, so it doesn't feel clinical. I'm also grateful it says "you need comfort" and not "you need healing". I'm a little worn out by healing talk, and this line doesn't push it at me. Psalm 102 fits my body too. "Withered like grass" and "I even forget to eat my bread" is what a bad flare feels like. Further on, the burning bones and days like a shadow are words I would never say to anyone at church. The turn in 102:17 promises that God hears the prayer of the worn-out and won't despise it. It does not promise that God will fix me. That is the honest comfort I actually want. I feel seen, not boxed in.
verdict.wouldHurt: Because the psalm is printed in full, I will reach 102:23-24: "He weakened my strength in the way; He shortened my days... take me not away in the midst of my days." With a chronic illness that line stings. It is honest lament and I would not want it cut, but a quiet word that the psalm keeps going past that point would help. "The destitute" in the turn line reads a little like poverty, not exhaustion, so it could feel slightly off at first glance.
verdict.theirSituation: A tired woman with a chronic illness who wants to be heard and comforted, not promised a cure.

results.desc: Mark, 57, Atlanta, Georgia, Baptist. He was laid off in June and the credit card debt is now about forty thousand dollars; nobody at church knows. He wakes at 3 a.m. doing sums in his head and feels like he failed his family.

answers.wanted: Really hard, and nobody knows. 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside' nearly fits because he hides it, but losing his job isn't fine on the outside.
They don't know what I'm going through
I've let my family down. The shame is about failing to provide, not about a sin or a wrong he did.

friction.note: There's no option for 'they don't know' or 'I'm hiding it from them'. For someone keeping a secret from his church, 'Fine' and 'Kind to me' both feel false, because they're kind only because they don't know.

This follow-up came up because he tapped 'Ashamed', but every option assumes the shame comes from a sin, a habit or God warning him. Shame about failing his family as a provider, or about being laid off, has no home here. 'A sense that God is warning me' could make a man already doing sums at 3 a.m. feel he's being accused.
The options make him choose between how bad things are and the fact that he's hiding it. He'd want to say both.
The key is 'heavy' but the label reads 'Sad'. That's fine for him, but 'Heavy' might fit weight-of-worry people better than 'Sad'.

results.overall: Quick, and most taps felt true (Getting worse, Anxious/Ashamed, Money, Silent, Help). He was pushed into 'close' where the quiz had no words for a secret burden that others don't know about, and where 'Ashamed' led straight to sin-shaped options when his shame is about failing to provide.

verdict.why: Line 1 hits the shame but calls it sin. Mark feels he failed his family, but losing his job was not a wrong he needs to confess. Seeing "You've done wrong" first would sting a little, as if the quiz read his layoff as a moral failure, so he says "Not quite." Line 2 describes him: he wakes at 3 a.m. doing sums and the worry won't settle. He'd say yes. "Why are you downcast, O my soul? ... Put your hope in God" is what a man lying awake needs said to him. Many Baptists already know the verse, so it lands as familiar and trustworthy, not strange. It speaks to him without lecturing, and the turn to hope helps. Line 3 would have been too generic.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing in Psalm 42 itself would hurt him. The problem is that the line before it ("You've done wrong... you're ashamed, and you want to come back") is the first line he sees. It can read as if the quiz treats a layoff and debt as sin, which feeds the belief he already has that he failed. Shame from circumstances needs its own line apart from guilt over a wrong, or Psalm 51 should not rank first when the answers point to a crisis at work or with money.
verdict.theirSituation: Mark was laid off and has $40k of debt he hides from his church. He can't sleep and feels ashamed that he let his family down, but he hasn't committed a sin he needs to repent of.

results.desc: Elena, 24, Bucharest, Romania, Orthodox. Her boyfriend of three years ended it, saying she was too religious and he couldn't see a future. She keeps looking at old photos, has skipped the Liturgy for three weeks, and doesn't quite know how she feels about God right now.

answers.wanted: Something hard happened a few weeks ago and I'm still in it (the breakup wasn't yesterday, but it isn't over either)
Someone I loved left me (and my friends have been kind). 'Far away, or gone' sounds more like distance or death than a breakup
I don't know how I feel about Him right now / confused. I have drifted (three weeks without the Liturgy), but the real feeling is not knowing
I don't know what to say to You, or: Why did following You cost me him?

friction.note: No option fits being left by someone. 'One person has turned on me' is too hostile for a breakup and 'Far away, or gone' reads like distance or death. Since he left because she was 'too religious', she might tap 'turned on me', and that would send her down the enemies path, which is not what she is living.
Her faith is the reason he ended it, but the quiz only asks 'Is your faith part of it?' after an 'against me'-type answer. Someone who lost a relationship because of their faith has no way to say so.
The choices are 'just happened', 'getting worse' and 'same'. None of them says 'it happened a few weeks ago and I'm still raw', which is where most heartbreak sits.

There is nothing for mixed or unsure feelings, like 'I don't know how I feel about Him' or 'a bit hurt by Him'. 'Drifted' puts the blame on her, and that feels a little like a box when she is really just confused.
'Someone or something I've lost' works, but it sounds like grief over a death. 'A relationship that ended' would feel more like her.
There is no option for having no words, like 'I don't know what to say.' That is often the honest answer for someone who has stopped praying for a while.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly gentle, and the feelings and 'what's on your mind' questions fit her well. But the quiz has no clear way to say 'someone I loved left me, partly because of my faith'. She had to piece her situation together from answers meant for enemies or grief, and the God question pushed her toward 'drifted' when she really feels unsure.

verdict.why: As Elena, I would say yes to the first line. "Weighed down or uneasy, and it won't settle" is how the last three weeks have felt. I keep going back to the photos, and I can't settle about God either. The line doesn't name the breakup, so it feels broad rather than sharp, but it doesn't misread me. Psalm 42 in full would land harder than the summary suggests. "My tears have been my food day and night" (42:3) fits the nights with the photos. "I used to go with the multitude... to the house of God" (42:4) would hit hard, because I have skipped the Liturgy for three weeks and miss it. It also names God feeling far away without blaming me. The turn, "Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him," is gentle: the psalmist is talking to his own sad soul, not being told off, and that suits me not knowing how I feel about God. Line 2 is close, but it treats my distance from God as forgetfulness to fix with blessing and thanks. That would feel slightly wrong while I'm grieving, and a bit like being told to cheer up. The fallback would also be acceptable, because it offers Psalm 42 as well.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. One small risk: my boyfriend left because I was "too religious," so if the page leaned hard on "put your hope in God" without the psalm's own tears and longing around it, it could feel like being told to just pray harder. Printing the psalm in full avoids this. The summary line alone does not.
verdict.theirSituation: A young Orthodox woman whose three-year relationship ended because he found her too religious. She is grieving, looking at old photos, has missed the Liturgy for three weeks and feels unsure and far from God.

results.desc: James, 66, Glasgow, Scotland, Church of Scotland. His younger brother has cut him off over their father's estate and has been telling the rest of the family things about him that aren't true. He is bitter about it, knows he's meant to forgive, and doesn't want to yet.

answers.wanted: Somewhere between 'Hard, but I'm getting by' and 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside'. Life carries on, but this sits in him.
'My family' or 'A family falling-out'. 'People in my life' is vague for his own brother.
Something like 'He's waiting on me' or 'I know what He'd ask of me, and I'm not ready'. He doesn't feel God is far away or displeased. He feels a nudge to forgive that he's putting off.
'Clear my name' fitted almost as well. What he'd really say is 'I know, but not yet', an honest refusal to forgive yet, and nothing offered covers it.
'What they're saying about me' is right. He might also want 'That it's my own brother'.
None of these. His 'it isn't fair' is about his brother and the estate, not the state of the world. He'd want 'It's personal, not the world' or a way to skip.

friction.note: Choosing 'It isn't fair.' sends him to a question about the world (bad people doing well, the strong pushing the weak around, Christians suffering), but his unfairness is a private family matter. He has to pick a world-level grievance he doesn't hold, and that could skew the result toward a psalm about the wicked prospering.

None of the options lets someone admit they don't want to forgive yet, which is exactly where he is. Every option is either a complaint or a pious line, so the honest middle ('I know what You're asking. Not yet.') is missing.
There is no option for 'I know what He wants from me and I'm resisting it'. 'Displeased with me' goes too far and 'Just there, in the background' doesn't go far enough.
'People in my life' feels generic for an estranged brother. There is nothing for family or a falling-out until the 'ended' follow-up, which he never sees because the rift isn't over.
A 66-year-old Scot might find 'Really hard' and 'Hard, but I'm getting by' a bit dramatic for a family feud. The inside/outside option is closer but reads as depression, not a grievance.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy for him. The people questions (one person turned on me, talking about me, family, what they're saying) fit his situation very well. But the draft never lets him say the true thing, that he's bitter and not ready to forgive. The 'It isn't fair' path then pushes him into a question about the world's injustice that has nothing to do with his brother.

verdict.why: Line 1 is the first one that is really me. "Your own people have turned on you" is my brother exactly, and Psalm 3 is David fleeing his own son, so it's a family betrayal and I'd feel that. As a Kirk man I know the psalms, and "the One who lifts my head" would land with me at 66. Line 2 misses. My brother isn't scheming, and he isn't shameless in that sense. Line 3 is about the wicked prospering, which isn't my trouble at all. Still, the match is only near enough. What's actually eating me is the lies he's telling the family, and the quiz never names that. "More and more others are rising up against you" overstates it too. My relatives aren't rising up against me. They're hearing falsehoods and going quiet on me. A line about being lied about to your own kin (Psalm 12 or 120 territory, or 55's "it was not an enemy, but you, my companion") would have got me exactly. Nothing touches my bitterness or my not wanting to forgive yet either. It won't wound me, but it won't reach that part of me.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds, but there are two small things. "More and more others are rising up against you" pushes my family into the enemy camp, and a bitter man will gladly take that, which isn't healthy. Printed in full, Psalm 3 ends with God striking enemies on the cheek and breaking the teeth of the wicked. Read by a man who doesn't want to forgive his brother, that can feel like permission to call him "the wicked" rather than a call to hand the matter to God. The quiet "Hard words" note under cursing psalms would help here.
verdict.theirSituation: His brother cut him off over their father's estate and has been spreading lies about him to the rest of the family, and he is bitter and not ready to forgive.

results.desc: Sofia, 15, São Paulo, Brazil, evangelical. A group of girls at school have started a group chat that mocks her, and screenshots keep getting passed around. Her parents don't know; she prays at night for it to stop and feels anxious every morning on the bus.

answers.wanted: Somewhere between 'about the same' and 'getting worse': it keeps going and more people keep seeing the screenshots
'Make it stop.' She has been praying that every night, and 'Help.' is the nearest option
'Girls at school' or 'Kids at school'. She was torn between this, 'A whole group of people' and 'Friends, or people I trusted', because they are a group of classmates
'I don't know.' She is not sure whether being evangelical is part of why they target her
