'Everyone seeing it' or 'The screenshots getting passed around'. That is between 'That it won't stop' and 'That it keeps growing'

friction.note: There is no word for embarrassed or humiliated, which is the main feeling for a teenager being mocked online. 'Ashamed' is the nearest, but picking it opens a follow-up about 'Something I did', which would feel as if the quiz blames her for being bullied.
The options mix who they are to her (family, friends) with where she knows them from (work or school). A group of classmates fits three options at once. The word 'work' is also odd for a 15-year-old.
None of the options is about the thing being public: screenshots shared around, and everyone seeing it. 'That it keeps growing' comes close but feels vague.
'Clear my name' sounds legal and adult. A teen would not say it, even though it is somewhat on topic here.
This is a yes/no question with no 'I'm not sure' option. A teenager often cannot tell why people are picking on her.

results.overall: The quiz felt quick and mostly fitted her. The season and people questions described her life well ('Fine on the outside, not on the inside', 'Making fun of me'). The follow-ups about who the bullies are and what hurts most sounded a bit adult, and none of them named school bullying online directly.

verdict.why: The first line is true of me. I feel anxious every morning on the bus and it doesn't go away, so I would tap "Yes, that's it" right away. The result fits better than the line does. Psalm 42 has "my enemies taunt me, saying 'Where is your God?'" (42:10), which is exactly the mocking I'm living with. "Why are you downcast, O my soul? Put your hope in God" is something I could say to myself on the bus. But the line only names the feeling. It never says anyone is mocking me, so I feel understood in my feelings more than in what is actually happening. Line 2 comes closer to my situation, but "scheming" sounds like adults plotting, not girls passing screenshots around. And I don't think God has forgotten me; I'm still praying every night. Line 3 is too general. The quiz should show 42:10 or say something about being mocked, so a kid being bullied can see it's about them.
verdict.theirSituation: I'm a 15-year-old being mocked in a group chat by girls at school, with screenshots passed around. My parents don't know, I pray at night for it to stop, and I'm anxious every morning. What I'm going through is being mocked, not just feeling uneasy.

results.desc: Luis, 41, Los Angeles, lapsed Catholic. Work is busy, the two kids have back-to-back activities, and the month has been fine, just full. He hasn't prayed properly in ages; God feels distant, but not in a painful way, more like an old friend he's lost touch with.

answers.wanted: Something milder like "Stretched" or "Busy but okay". "Worn out" makes it sound worse than it is, but nothing else on the list fits a full, fine month.
"My family / the kids" (the running around, not a worry). Work is only half of it. "Someone I love" sounded like something was wrong with them, so I didn't tap it.
Something like "Hey, it's been a while." "I miss You" is the nearest, but it's more emotional than I actually feel. Everything else is for a crisis or a big moment.

friction.note: Almost every word is either a strong negative or a strong positive. Someone whose life is simply full and fine has nothing neutral to pick, like "Busy", "Stretched" or "Fine", so they end up choosing "Worn out", which overstates it.
There is no "Family / home life" option. For a parent, the kids' schedules are the main thing on their mind. "Someone I love" reads as though someone is in trouble.

The list leans heavily toward distress (How long? Why? Help. Clear my name. It isn't fair.) and devotion (How great You are). For a lapsed, drifting person there is no casual, reconnecting line. "Clear my name" in particular is baffling out of context.
"Displeased with me" might sting a little for a lapsed Catholic, like a guilt trip. Not a real problem, but noticeable. "I've drifted from Him" fitted perfectly, though.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy. The season, trend, people and God questions described Luis's month well, but the feelings list and the \"say to Him\" list are built for people in pain or on a high, so an ordinary busy, drifting month had to be stretched to fit.

verdict.why: Line 1 is not me. I'm not longing or fainting for anything; that's too intense for where I am, and I'd tap "Not quite" right away. Line 2 hits: "God has slipped into the background" is exactly how it feels. It's not a crisis, just busyness and drift, and "slipped" doesn't blame me or make it sound worse than it is. "Want to wake your soul up to Him again" goes a little further than I'd say out loud, but I'm taking this quiz, so part of me does. I'd say yes. Psalm 103 fits well. "Bless the LORD, O my soul" is a line you say to yourself, like a nudge, and "do not forget all His kind deeds" lands for a guy whose life is fine, full and blessed but who has stopped noticing. The advice about giving thanks "through everything and in everything" suits a month that was good but rushed. It would probably make me want to read the rest, and maybe say it in the car between practices. Line 3, being worn down and empty, would have been a misread. I'm busy, not depleted. So I'm glad it came third and not first.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. The only soft spot is that "you want to wake your soul up" assumes I've already decided to come back. For a lapsed Catholic who is only half-curious, that is a little ahead of me. Something like "and part of you would like to wake up to Him again" would fit better.
verdict.theirSituation: A full, fine life has pushed God into the background. There's no pain in it, just distance, and he's mildly curious about reconnecting.

results.desc: Hannah, 33, Leeds, UK, Baptist. Her first baby is six weeks old, and she is exhausted and very happy in about equal measure. She can't concentrate long enough to pray and feels a bit guilty that she hasn't been to church since the birth.

answers.wanted: Exhausting but lovely. It's not really up and down, it's both at once, all day.
I haven't had the headspace for Him. Not far, I just can't sit still long enough to pray, and I feel a bit guilty about it.
Thank You, and I'm so tired. Both at once. I'd want to pick two here like on the feelings question.

friction.note: 'Up and down' suggests swings between good and bad days. A new parent is tired and happy at the same moment. No option says 'Hard and wonderful at once'.

Nothing fits 'I've had no time or headspace for God'. 'I've drifted from Him' sounds like a spiritual failing and would make her feel judged. 'Just there, in the background' is near enough but a bit flat for someone who still believes.
Only one pick here, but her honest prayer is 'thank You' and 'I'm so tired' together. Being made to choose one loses half of what she feels.
Her small guilt about prayer and church has nowhere to go. 'Ashamed' is far too strong, so she won't tap it, and the guilt is never picked up.

'They're new in my life' is a bit cool for a newborn, but she'd get it right away. The options just before it ('I'm losing them', 'They're ill, or in danger') are hard to read for a new mum with a six-week-old, though she can skip past them.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy to answer on a phone while holding a baby. The good-news path (new, happy, someone new in my life, a new family) fitted well. The only snag was that the tired half and the gently guilty half of her life only fitted where two picks were allowed, and the God question had no kind way to say 'no time to pray right now'.

verdict.why: Line 1 catches the guilty part. I can't pray and I haven't been to church, and I do want to get back to Him. So I'd tap yes, though it doesn't quite fit. God hasn't slipped away because I drifted. I'm just too tired to hold a thought. If I had said no, line 2 ("thank God in and through everything") would have caught the joy, and it leads to the same psalm anyway. Psalm 103 is a lovely landing for a new mum. It turns my scattered prayer into a short call to my own soul to "bless the LORD" and not forget His kindness, and I have a lot to be grateful for right now. The full psalm also has the lines about a father's compassion for his children and God knowing we are dust, which would make me cry in a good way at 3am. I'd feel seen and not told off. Psalm 102 (withered, empty) would have been wrong for me: I'm tired, not empty.
verdict.wouldHurt: "God has slipped into the background" leans a little toward drifting or spiritual neglect. For a new mum who already feels guilty about missing church and prayer, it could add to the guilt, because what's really going on is exhaustion, not coldness. Something gentler, like "you're too worn out to pray the way you used to", would fit her better. Nothing in the psalm itself would hurt.
verdict.theirSituation: She's a happy, exhausted new mother who can't focus to pray and feels guilty about it, but her faith hasn't cooled. She's grateful and running on no sleep.

results.desc: Chidi, 27, Lagos, Nigeria, Anglican. He just accepted a job in Abuja and is moving next month, leaving friends and his church behind. He is excited and nervous and already feels a bit lonely thinking about starting over.

answers.wanted: Exciting but unsettling: a big change is coming
Excited and nervous (and a bit lonely, but only two picks allowed)
Kind to me, but I'm about to leave them behind

friction.note: Nothing for a season of transition. A big move that is exciting and scary at once isn't really 'Up and down', and it isn't just 'Good' either.

No 'Excited' or 'Nervous'. 'Anxious' feels heavier than first-week-at-a-new-job nerves. With only two picks he had to drop 'Lonely', and the loneliness is the part he would most want the psalm to speak to.
No option for 'good people, but I'm leaving them'. 'Far away, or gone' is wrong because they are still here, at least for now.
'A new home, or a new family' tempted him, but 'new family' reads as marriage or a baby. 'A new place, a new start' would fit a move far better.
'Something new is starting' fitted well. It was the only place the move showed up clearly.

results.overall: It was quick, friendly and nothing felt preachy. But it is built mostly around trouble, so a hopeful-but-nervous life change had to be squeezed into answers like 'Up and down' and 'Anxious'. He finished unsure whether the quiz had picked up on the loneliness of starting over.

verdict.why: Line 1 misses Chidi. He is nervous, not "tired of living afraid", and nothing in his life calls for helping others take heart. Line 2 is half right: he is uneasy. But "weighed down" and "won't settle" describe something heavier and more stuck than an exciting move he chose, so he would hesitate and pass. Line 3 fits best. He has just accepted a job, is being led to a new city and is mostly glad. "Guided on your way" reads like a move, and Psalm 23 carries the nervousness too: the valley, "I will fear no evil", "Thou art with me". He would say yes and be glad he got there. Two problems for the test. First, the ranking is backwards for him: the most fitting line came last, after two lines about fear and heaviness. A more anxious tapper might accept line 2 and get a psalm about depression that he doesn't have. Second, none of the lines names what makes this moment his own: leaving friends and his church and starting over alone. So he feels mostly seen, but through the glad side only.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing in Psalm 23 would hurt him. The risk is the order: if he had accepted line 2, Psalm 42's "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" would make his excitement look like despair. Line 1's "tired of living afraid" also slightly overstates ordinary nerves.
verdict.theirSituation: He is making a hopeful move he chose, to a new city and a new job, and it is bittersweet: he is excited and nervous, and lonely at leaving his friends and his church.

results.desc: Margaret, 68, Des Moines, Iowa, Lutheran. She retired from teaching in June after thirty-eight years, and the days feel shapeless. She is grateful and rested, but she keeps wondering what she's actually for now.

answers.wanted: A big change I'm still getting used to. Retirement started in June, but it doesn't feel like 'something new starting' so much as something ending and nothing yet in its place.
At loose ends, or adrift. Grateful is right, but 'Unsure' is only near. She isn't unsure about a decision; her days just have no shape or purpose.

Rest after a long job well done: thirty-eight years of teaching behind me and time to breathe. None of the options is about a finished life's work or finally having rest, so she settles for 'Everything, really'.

friction.note: Picking 'Something new is starting' triggers 'What's behind the good?', which assumes the new thing is good. That fits her, but someone whose new start is frightening would feel boxed in. The options (a new home, coming to faith, coming back to Him, answered prayer) are all about gaining something. None covers an ending you are thankful for, like retirement, graduation or a finished task, or simply having rest.
Nothing fits a transition that is neither over nor starting, the in-between after a big change. 'Something new is starting' sounds more hopeful than she feels about the shapeless days.

The word list has no 'adrift', 'aimless' or 'purposeless', which is the main feeling of a new retiree, an empty-nester or someone just laid off. 'Restless' and 'Unsure' come close but mean something else.
'What's next for me' fits, but her real question is 'what am I for now', which is about purpose and usefulness, not plans. A little narrow, but workable.
'Just there, in the background' could read as a mild confession of lukewarmness. A Lutheran who is content but not stirred might hesitate over whether that is a criticism.

'Make me who You want me to be' sounds a little more like church talk than the other options. Out of context, 'How long?' and 'Clear my name.' read oddly for someone in a calm season, though that is fine because she skips them.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy. She found a close answer for everything and several fitted exactly. But the quiz seemed built for people in trouble or in joy, and her in-between state (grateful, rested, but wondering what she is for now) never got a clean option; her feeling of losing purpose had no word of its own.

verdict.why: As Margaret, the first line is the one I'd say yes to, because "what am I for now?" is exactly something I can't work out on my own and would bring to God. The verses shown are right for me: "Teach me the way I should walk" and "Teach me to do Your will... lead me on level ground" put words to my question better than I could. Line 2 is also true, since I am grateful, but thanking God isn't what's pressing on me right now. So I'd pass it over, though it would have been a pleasant second choice. The line itself is a bit vague ("something you can't work out") and doesn't name a new season of life or a question of purpose. I only recognise myself because the verse under it does that work.
verdict.wouldHurt: When the whole of Psalm 143 is printed, it opens on an enemy who "has crushed my life to the ground" and "made me dwell in darkness like those long dead", with a spirit that "fails" and a heart "dismayed". I'm rested and content, just unsure of my purpose, and reading that makes the result feel like it took me for someone in anguish. The "long dead" line lands oddly for a 68-year-old just past retirement. The verses I'd want (8 and 10) are there, but I'd have to wade through a lament to reach them. A note that points me to those verses as my part of the psalm would help. The "Plead" wording in Athanasius's advice also feels heavier than what I'm going through.
verdict.theirSituation: She's a retired teacher who is content and grateful, but after decades of work she has lost her sense of purpose and is asking God what He wants her for next. She is not in distress.

results.desc: Nikos, 45, Athens, Greece, nominal Orthodox. He goes to church at Easter and for weddings and funerals, and lately he's been reading about science and wondering whether any of it holds up. He isn't upset, just unsure, and quietly curious whether God is there at all.

answers.wanted: Big questions: whether God is real, whether any of it holds up next to science

friction.note: "God, and my faith" assumes he has a faith to worry about. For a nominal believer whose question is whether any of it is true, "my faith" feels slightly off. Something like "Big questions: God, meaning, whether it's true" would fit someone curious rather than troubled.

Asking what he would say to Him assumes someone is listening, and he isn't sure anyone is. "Are You there?" rescues it, but he might hesitate at the question itself. A lead-in such as "If anyone's listening..." would feel less like being put in a box.

"I'm not sure He's there" fits well. With nothing but "Close" and "Clearly at work" around it, though, this reads as a list of feelings for believers. Nothing there is for intellectual curiosity. What he feels about God isn't far or silent, just undecided.
Nothing so far sounds preachy. His worry is that the result will read his curiosity as suffering or spiritual crisis. He isn't upset, and most of the options lean toward trouble or toward devotion.

results.overall: Quick and mostly painless. The questions were plain enough, and "Curious", "Unsure" and "Are You there?" let him answer honestly. He would note that the quiz seems built for believers going through a hard time rather than for a calm skeptic. He is curious whether the psalm he gets will speak to honest doubt rather than to distress.

verdict.why: Nikos would pass the first line with some hesitation. "Losing your footing" sounds more dramatic than what he feels, because he is curious, not in crisis. Still, his faith has quietly slipped, and "honest enough to admit it" names the honesty of his doubt without scolding him. Psalm 73 is a psalm about nearly losing faith, told from the inside by someone who is surprised to find God still holding on to him. For a doubter that is a gentle, credible text: it does not argue with science, it simply shows that doubt has a place inside the Psalms. He would reject line 2. He isn't marvelling at God's care or His commands; he is asking whether God is there at all. Oddly, Psalm 19's "the heavens declare" suits someone reading science better than the line in front of it does, but the line takes for granted a belief he does not hold yet. The fallback would be a poor fit. None of its three options (grinding, weighing, afraid) is true of him, since he isn't upset.
verdict.wouldHurt: It wouldn't wound him, but it would slightly misread him. "Come close to losing your footing" and Athanasius's "whatever in you has slipped" suggest a fall or a moral lapse. His real state is calm, intellectual uncertainty. Psalm 73 is also about envying the wicked who prosper, which is not his question, so parts of the full text would feel beside the point. The turn at 73:23 ("You hold my right hand") assumes God is there, and a sceptic might read that as the quiz answering his question for him. None of the lines names plain, calm doubt about whether God exists.
verdict.theirSituation: He isn't in distress. He is calmly and intellectually unsure whether God exists, pulled by his science reading and quietly hoping to find there is something to it.

results.desc: Ana, 36, Manila, Philippines, Catholic. Life is steady: work, family, the usual. She still says the rosary most nights out of habit but has felt nothing for months, and she wonders whether that's normal or whether something is wrong with her.

answers.wanted: I pray, but I don't feel anything anymore
Is it normal to feel nothing? / Is something wrong with me?

friction.note: 'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' is about unanswered requests. Her problem is that prayer feels empty: she keeps praying and feels nothing. No option names that plain dryness. 'Far away' and 'I'm not sure He's there' both claim more than she feels, since she isn't doubting.

Her real question is 'Is this normal?' or 'What's wrong with me?', and neither is listed. 'Are You there?' sounds like doubting God exists, which isn't where she is. 'I miss You' assumes she feels a longing, but she feels numb.

There's a small pull between 'Quiet and ordinary' and 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside'. Her life really is ordinary, but 'not on the inside' sounds like distress, which overstates a flat, dry prayer life. Nothing sits between the two.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly easy until the two God questions. Neither had a plain option for a faithful routine that feels empty, so she had to pick answers that sound either more doubting or more hurt than she is.

verdict.why: Neither line describes Ana. Line 1 is about almost slipping or losing faith, but she hasn't. She keeps praying out of faithful habit, and being told she nearly stumbled would feel like an accusation. Line 2 gets "empty" right, but it blames life wearing her down, and her life is steady. Her problem is not hardship. It is dryness in prayer: she prays and feels nothing, and she wants to know whether that is normal. So she would tap "Not quite" on both. The honest fallback works better than either line. Of its three options, "It's weighing on me, and it won't lift" (Psalm 42) comes closest. Psalm 42 is the classic psalm of spiritual thirst: "my soul thirsts for God... why are you cast down, O my soul... hope in God." It would answer her real question (you are not broken; the psalmist felt this too), even though "weighing on me" overstates how she feels. She is puzzled more than burdened. The quiz lacks a line for "I keep praying but feel nothing / God feels far or silent." That is a very common situation for practising Catholics, and it deserves its own route, ideally to Psalm 42 or Psalm 63.
verdict.wouldHurt: Line 1 ("come close to losing your footing") could read as a verdict that her dryness is a spiritual failing. That is the exact fear she brought to the quiz.
verdict.theirSituation: She is a faithful Catholic whose life is steady. She keeps praying the rosary but has felt nothing for months, and she wants to know whether that dryness is normal or a sign that something is wrong with her.

results.desc: Ben, 22, Minneapolis, Minnesota, became a Christian six months ago through a campus group. The early excitement has worn off and he's not sure he is doing it right; reading the Bible is harder than he expected. He believes, but God feels quieter than at the start.

answers.wanted: Kind of flat after a big start
The excitement has worn off
Quieter than He used to be

friction.note: Nothing covers 'quieter than at the start'. 'Near, but quiet' claims nearness he isn't sure he feels, 'Far away' is too strong, and 'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' sounds like unanswered prayer for a crisis, not a spark fading. A new believer would want an option that compares now with before.
No option fits 'the first excitement has faded'. 'About the same' misses the slow cooling, and 'Something new is starting' describes six months ago, not now.
The options measure how hard life is. His life isn't hard; his faith feels flat. 'Up and down' was the nearest, but it's a guess.
There is nothing for 'Am I doing this right?', which is his real question. 'Show me the way' is near, but it sounds more like asking for life direction than asking how to read the Bible or pray.

results.overall: It was quick and easy to tap through, and none of it felt preachy. But the quiz seems built for people going through hardship, not for a young believer whose faith has gone flat. No follow-up question came up for him, so his result rests on a few near-miss answers, and he'd wonder whether it really understood where he is.

verdict.why: As Ben, line 1 is too strong. I haven't nearly fallen away. I'm just unsure, and saying yes to it would feel like confessing to backsliding I haven't done. Line 2 is the first one I'd say yes to. My real question is "am I doing this right?", and Psalm 143:8 and 143:10 ("Teach me the way I should walk", "Teach me to do Your will... lead me on level ground") are almost word for word what I'd pray. The line itself is vague, though. "Something you can't work out on your own" could mean anything, so I'd say yes because of the psalm more than because of the line. What it misses is the part that bothers me most: God feels quieter than he did at the start. Psalm 42 fits that best, since it's about thirsting for God's presence and asking "where is your God?". But line 3 frames 42 as being "weighed down or uneasy", which sounds heavier than what I feel, so I'd skip past it. I'd feel mostly seen, and a bit boxed in by how dramatic the options are.
verdict.wouldHurt: Psalm 143 printed in full includes lines like "the enemy has pursued my soul, crushing my life to the ground" and "my spirit is faint", which overshoot a mild season of uncertainty and could make a new believer wonder if things are worse than he thought. Line 1 ("come close to losing your footing") is shown first and could read as calling a new Christian's quiet doubts backsliding. And nothing names spiritual dryness or God seeming quieter, which is the most common thing new believers go through.
verdict.theirSituation: He's a new believer six months in: the first excitement is gone, God seems quieter, reading the Bible is hard, and he mainly wants to know how to walk this faith rightly. He isn't in distress or close to falling away.

results.desc: Ruth, 50, Bristol, UK, Methodist. Her fourteen-year-old dog has kidney failure and the vet says it's probably a matter of weeks. Otherwise life is fine, but she feels silly for how much it's weighing on her and hasn't mentioned it to anyone but her sister.

answers.wanted: Something between 'something hard just happened' and 'getting worse': 'I've had bad news and it's coming'
'A pet' or 'Someone I'm about to lose'. She hesitates over whether a dog counts as 'someone I love', and 'Someone or something I've lost' is past tense, so it doesn't fit yet
Something like 'Give me strength for what's coming' or 'Be with her at the end'. 'Stay with me' was nearly as good

friction.note: Nothing clearly covers a pet. 'Someone I love' sounds like a person, so she wonders whether she is using the quiz wrong, and that feeds the 'I'm being silly' feeling she already has. 'Someone or something I've lost' is past tense and doesn't fit a loss she can see coming.
There is no option for grief you can see coming (bad news, and the end is weeks away). 'Something hard just happened' and 'Getting worse' each catch only half of it.
'I'm losing them' fits well. 'They're ill, or in danger' fits too, and she might hesitate between the two. The options assume the loved one is a person ('new in my life', 'in need').

The list leans towards crisis ('How long?', 'Clear my name.', 'It isn't fair.'). For a quiet, private grief, nothing gentle like 'Give me strength' or 'Hold what I love' is offered, so 'Help.' feels bigger than what she means.

Nothing lets her say 'this is small next to other people's troubles'. If the result reads like a psalm for great distress, she may feel it is overblown for a dog, or feel that her grief is being made fun of.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and mostly easy, and 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside' and 'I'm losing them' fitted her closely. The hardest moment was the focus question: with no clear place for a dying pet, she wondered whether her grief belonged in the quiz at all.

verdict.why: As Ruth, I'd tap "Yes, that's it" on the first line. It's heavy and it won't lift, and it doesn't make me say "grief", which I'd feel a bit silly saying about a dog. It also doesn't make me explain why it matters so much. "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" is a question I could say to myself without feeling daft, and "Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him" is gentle rather than scolding. The advice that "what grieves you is healed" as you speak to your own soul would comfort me. It doesn't have to be about a person for this to count. Line 2 (pleading) is a bit off: I'm not really bargaining, as the vet has been clear. Line 3 (God slipping into the background) doesn't fit at all. One small miss: "uneasy... won't settle" sounds more like anxiety than sadness at a slow goodbye. The rest of Psalm 42, about longing for God and people asking "Where is your God?", is more than I'm carrying, so parts of it will feel like someone else's trouble. The opening and turning verses still land.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. If the full Psalm 42 page leans hard on enemies taunting "Where is your God?" or on being far from God, it might feel a size too big for grief over a pet. But it doesn't mock the grief or play it down.
verdict.theirSituation: She is sad ahead of time about losing her old dog within weeks, and feels embarrassed that it weighs on her this much. It's sorrow and a quiet heaviness, not restless unease.

results.desc: Mina, 31, Cairo, Egypt, Coptic Orthodox. It has been an ordinary, slightly boring week: work, the gym, dinner with his parents on Friday. Nothing is wrong, but everything feels like routine, and he wonders if there's meant to be more to faith than turning up.

answers.wanted: Bored, or 'going through the motions'. Restless is near, but he isn't agitated, just flat.
Something like 'Whether there's more to life than this'. It isn't pressing on him the way 'God, and my faith' sounds, and 'Nothing in particular' would hide the real question.
'Is this all there is?' or 'Wake me up.' Show me the way is the nearest, but he isn't lost or at a crossroads, just stuck in routine.

friction.note: Seventeen words and nothing for boredom or flatness. For someone whose week is just routine, 'Numb' is too dark and 'At peace' is too rosy, so he ends up choosing 'Restless' even though it overstates things.

Most of the fourteen options are about crisis (How long?, Why?, Help., I'm so tired., Clear my name., It isn't fair.). On an ordinary week the list reads as if something is supposed to be wrong. None of the lines fits the everyday feeling of 'I show up, but is this it?'
'God, and my faith' sounds like a big spiritual preoccupation. His question is quieter than that, so tapping it feels like claiming more than is true.
'About the same' fits. The other five options all describe change, so a steady life has only one place to go. That's fine, just slightly thin.

results.overall: For Mina it was quick and mostly natural. 'Quiet and ordinary' and 'Just there, in the background' described his week exactly. The emotion and prayer questions are built around trouble or joy, though, so a merely routine week had to be pushed into 'Restless' and 'Show me the way'.

verdict.why: Line 1 is about nearly falling, and nothing in my week is that dramatic. Saying yes to it would mean admitting a crisis I don't have. Line 2 is the first one that catches me. God hasn't gone anywhere; I still turn up. But He has become the background to work, the gym and Friday dinner, and part of me wants to be woken up. Psalm 103, "Bless the Lord, O my soul... forget not all His benefits," is the right answer to routine. It doesn't scold me for being bored. It tells me to stir up my own soul and remember, and that's an active step I can take this week. I pray this psalm in the Agpeya, so meeting it here feels familiar and trustworthy, not like a label stuck on me. Athanasius's line about giving thanks through everything and in everything answers my question of whether there's more to faith than turning up: the more is in how you turn up.
verdict.wouldHurt: It hurts nothing, but two small things feel slightly off. First, the numbering. As a Copt I pray with the Septuagint numbers, so to me this psalm is 102, and 103 is "Bless the Lord, O my soul... You are clothed with honour and majesty." Seeing "Psalms 103 and 104" with no note on the numbering could confuse me for a moment. Second, "slipped into the background" leans a little toward saying I've drifted, when my honest feeling is that my faith is flat and routine, not that I've wandered away. The line is close enough that I'd still tap yes.
verdict.theirSituation: Nothing is wrong. His faith has gone flat and routine, and he wonders whether there should be more to it than showing up.

results.desc: Carmen, 63, Lima, Peru, Catholic. Her daughter started speaking to her again after six years apart, and they had lunch last week. She is happy and thankful, but the conversation was awkward and some of the old hurt is still there on both sides.

answers.wanted: Good, but tender. Happy, with old hurt still there
Someone who was gone has come back, but it's still awkward
We're finally talking again after years apart, and we're healing slowly

friction.note: No option for a relationship being mended. 'They're doing well' is about the daughter, not the two of them, and 'I'm losing them' is the reverse. A mother whose child has come back has nothing to tap here, and this is her whole situation.

The options are either hostile or simply nice. Nothing fits 'someone came back, and it's good but uneasy'. 'Hard to be around' would sound like an accusation against her daughter, so she would never tap it.

'Something hard is finally over' feels too final when the hurt is still there, and 'Getting better' leaves out that a long break has just ended. Something like 'Something is starting to heal' would fit.
'Up and down' sounds more troubled than she feels, and 'Good' leaves out the awkwardness. Nothing covers 'happy but tender'.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and warm, and the feelings, God and 'Thank You' questions fit her well. But her real story is a daughter who came back after six years, and neither the people question nor the 'someone I love' follow-up has a place for mending a relationship, so she would feel she had to half-describe it.

verdict.why: Carmen's main feeling right now is gratitude. After six years her daughter is speaking to her again, and "thank God, in and through everything" fits a thankfulness that has to include the awkward lunch and the old hurt, not just the good part. She would say yes to it. Psalm 103 then gives her more than the line promised. It has "as far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions", "He will not always accuse", and "as a father has compassion on his children". For a mother who has just started mending things with her child, those lines speak straight to the forgiveness still to be worked out on both sides. The second line, about God's kindness to everyone, is too general for her. It says nothing about her own situation.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing would wound her. The only gap is that the line she chooses mentions only thanks. It does not name the mixed part: the reconciliation that is still tender and the hurt still there. She might briefly feel that half of her story went unseen, until she reads the forgiveness verses in the psalm itself.
verdict.theirSituation: She is thankful that her daughter has come back after six years, but it is still fragile and the old hurt is there on both sides, so what she feels is gratitude mixed with wanting healing and forgiveness.

results.desc: Samuel, 38, Chennai, India, Church of South India. He has a job offer in Dubai with much better pay, but it means leaving his aging parents and his wife's family. He has been praying about it for weeks and feels no clear answer either way.

answers.wanted: At a crossroads / facing a big decision
A big choice is in front of me (nothing has started yet, it's only an offer)
A big decision: my family versus a better job
I keep asking and get no clear answer (quiet on this one question, not absent)
I'm not sure it is good yet; it's a choice I have to make. Or: 'Nothing yet, I'm still deciding'

friction.note: He got this question only because he tapped 'Something new is starting'. It assumes the new thing is good. For him it's an undecided offer with a real cost (leaving his aging parents), so 'What's behind the good?' feels presumptuous. Every option is upbeat, so he has to pretend to be thankful. It needs a 'not sure it's good yet' option, or it shouldn't be asked when the other answers are unsure or anxious.
None of the eight options says 'at a crossroads' or 'a big decision to make', and that's the most common reason someone asks what psalm they're living. 'Up and down' is a guess.
'Something new is starting' sounds like it's already decided. He hasn't accepted the job. 'A decision is coming' would fit many people.

'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' is about suffering that doesn't lift. His case is prayer for guidance with no clear answer, which is a different experience. The words push him toward a lament he doesn't feel.

'What's next for me' fits loosely, but the pull is between family duty and opportunity. Parents plus 'what's next' can't both be picked. Letting people pick two here, as other questions do, would help.

results.overall: Quick, and it mostly felt respectful. 'Unsure', 'Anxious' and 'Show me the way' fit him exactly. But the quiz has no way to say 'I'm facing a hard decision'. So Samuel ended up on the good-news branch, having to name something good he's thankful for when he's actually torn.

verdict.why: Line 1 is partly true: I am uneasy and it won't settle. But I am not downcast. I have a good offer and a good family, and the trouble is not knowing which way to go. So I would say "Not quite" to it, with some hesitation. Line 2 describes my weeks of prayer exactly: I cannot work this out on my own and I keep laying it before God. Psalm 143:8, "Teach me the way I should walk," is the very prayer I have been praying, and 143:10, "lead me on level ground," fits a man who has to choose between two roads. I would feel seen, and I would probably save this verse.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds, but two things fall flat. First, Athanasius's advice for this result is thin compared with the others ("When you want to plead with God and pray, you have Psalms 5 and 143"). It reads like a catalogue entry, not like words spoken to me. Second, if the full psalm is printed, verse 3 ("the enemy pursues my soul, crushing my life to the ground") and the closing request to destroy enemies do not fit a peaceful choice about a job. Without a short note that the psalm's heart for me is verses 8 and 10, it could feel like the quiz mistook my dilemma for persecution.
verdict.theirSituation: He is torn over a job abroad that would take him away from his aging parents and his in-laws, and he has had no clear answer after weeks of prayer. He needs guidance more than comfort.

results.desc: Kayla, 17, Savannah, Georgia, grew up going to a Methodist church. She is stressed about college applications and her SAT scores, but otherwise things are fine with friends and family. She believes in God, though right now it's more background than anything she thinks about.

answers.wanted: Stressful, but nothing's actually wrong
College applications. It's both 'Work or school' and 'What's next for me', and she'd hesitate between them
Let this work out / Let me get in. Half-wanted 'Show me the way.' too, but only one tap is allowed

friction.note: There's no option for 'stressed but okay'. 'Busy, but fine' downplays the stress and 'Hard, but I'm getting by' overstates it. A teen with exam stress sits between the two.
'Work or school' and 'What's next for me' overlap for a college applicant, so she can't tell which one the quiz means and may worry she's picking the 'wrong' one.

The question takes for granted that she talks to God. For someone who keeps Him in the background it feels like a slight push. 'Make me who You want me to be.' and 'How great You are.' read as churchy and preachy to a 17-year-old, and 'Clear my name.' would confuse her because it's unclear what situation it means.
With only one pick, she has to choose between 'Help.' and 'Show me the way.', which both fit. Allowing one or two picks, as on the feelings question, would fit better.
'Displeased with me' and 'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' are heavy, but the option list is fair overall. 'Just there, in the background' fitted her exactly, and that made her feel understood.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and mostly easy for Kayla, and none of the follow-ups applied to her. Her real situation, ordinary school stress, only got 'close' matches on the season and focus questions. The last question, what to say to God, felt a little churchier than where she is right now.

verdict.why: Line 1 overshoots. I'm stressed, not empty or listless, and "forget to eat my bread" or "withered like grass" sounds like depression, so I'd tap Not quite. Line 2 fits closely enough: SAT scores and applications keep buzzing in my head and I can't settle, so I'd tap Yes. The honest part of line 3 (God is in the background for me) is true too, but I didn't come here looking to wake anything up, so I never get to it. Psalm 42's "Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God" is a line I could screenshot before a test. Most of the psalm is about thirsting for God and being taunted, which is bigger than my problem, but it isn't off-putting. The weak spot is the order. The quiz put the heaviest reading first for someone whose worry is ordinary pressure about the future.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds me. The word "downcast" and the psalm's heavier lines (tears day and night, enemies taunting) are bigger than a stressed teenager's week and could feel slightly melodramatic. Seeing Psalm 102 offered first could make me think the quiz decided I'm depressed.
verdict.theirSituation: She is anxious about her future and her performance (college applications, SAT scores) and isn't depressed or in crisis. Faith sits quietly in the background, and she would most want a psalm about trusting God with what's ahead, not one about being worn down.

results.desc: Paul, 60, Birmingham, Alabama, Episcopalian. He picked up his five-year sobriety chip last week, and his grown son came to watch. He feels grateful in a way that still surprises him and wants to keep saying thank you to God.

answers.wanted: Something I worked hard for just came through: five years sober, with my son there to see it
My recovery / staying sober. It is really about God and about my son, but neither option alone names it
Getting free of something that had hold of me, by His grace, one day at a time (a rescue or deliverance that keeps going, not a single answered prayer)

friction.note: 'Something I've done' sounds like guilt only. A man in recovery would think of his sobriety as 'something I've done', but the wording suggests wrongdoing, so he steers away from it. There is no option for a milestone or an achievement.

'Something hard is finally over' is close but not right, because recovery is never 'over', and an AA member would bristle at being told it is. Between 'Getting better' and 'over' there is nothing for 'a long fight that is holding'.

There is no option for deliverance from an addiction or a habit. 'Coming back to Him' and 'I'm growing' both brush against it but miss. He would expect a quiz about thanking God to have a 'He set me free' answer.
There is no option for a relationship that has been mended ('someone I'd hurt is back in my life'). 'A real gift' covers it well enough, but the reconciliation with his son is the heart of it.

results.overall: Quick and pleasant. The grateful answers (Good, Grateful, Kind, Clearly at work, Thank You) were easy and felt honest. What he actually wanted to say, that he got sober and the family he hurt came back, had no clear home in the focus or 'what's behind the good' options. So he ended up close instead of seen.

verdict.why: Paul wants to keep thanking God, and line 1 says exactly that, so he would say "Yes, that's it" on the first try. Psalm 103 fits him closely. Just after the verse shown, it says God "forgives all your iniquities, heals all your diseases, redeems your life from the pit." For a man with five years sober and a son back at his side, those lines describe his own recovery. As an Episcopalian he will know this psalm from the Prayer Book, so it will feel familiar. Line 2 would also fit, but line 1 is closer, because his thankfulness is personal ("do not forget all His kind deeds") more than wonder at God's goodness to everyone.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. One small point: the prompt "in and through everything" is a little abstract and says nothing about the specific rescue he is thankful for. The psalm's own verses about redemption from the pit fill that gap, so the full printed text matters more here than the one-line summary.
verdict.theirSituation: Paul is grateful for his recovery and his restored relationship with his son, and he wants to keep thanking God.

results.desc: Esther, 29, Kumasi, Ghana, Methodist. After two years of trying, she and her husband found out she is pregnant. She keeps thinking about all the months she prayed for this and feels that God really did hear her.

answers.wanted: Both at once: the long wait is over AND something new (a baby) is starting. I'd want to tap both.
The baby coming / becoming a family. Nothing says that, so I picked God because I keep thinking He heard me; 'What's next for me' was the other near one.

friction.note: 'Something hard is finally over' and 'Something new is starting' are both true for her, and she can only pick one. Picking 'over' also seems to skip the 'What's behind the good?' question. That question has 'An answered prayer' and 'A new home, or a new family', which fit her better than anything else in the quiz.
The routing looks like a gap: season 'Really good' + grateful/happy + trend 'over' never reaches 'What's behind the good?'. A joyful person whose trouble just ended probably should get it.

Nothing fits a joyful family event like a pregnancy, a wedding or a new baby. 'Someone I love' leads to a follow-up that is mostly about suffering, and 'What's next for me' sounds like a career worry.

'A long wait' fits her, but calling two years of trying for a baby 'something hard' is fair. No problem, just a note that infertility isn't named. That's probably wise, since it keeps the quiz from feeling like it's probing.
'I prayed, and He answered' fits her exactly. It feels good to see that option, not preachy.

results.overall: For her the quiz is warm and quick. Most taps fit exactly, and 'I prayed, and He answered' says it for her. Two things bothered her: she had to pick between 'over' and 'new' when both are true, and nothing names the good news itself (a baby, a new family).

verdict.why: Esther wants to thank God and bless Him, and the first line says so. Psalm 103 fits her well. "Do not forget all His kind deeds" matches her remembering the months she prayed. Later the psalm says He satisfies you with good things, forgives, heals, and has compassion as a father does, which fits a woman expecting her first child after long waiting. The line itself is a bit general. "In and through everything" suggests keeping a thankful habit through good times and bad, while her feeling is more specific: God heard this particular prayer. She would still say "Yes, that's it" without hesitating. Line 2 would also be close. She did go to God over and over, and she does want to tell people. But Psalm 46's "refuge… in times of trouble" makes her infertility sound like a siege, which is a less natural fit than plain thanksgiving. The quiz has no line for "God answered the prayer I kept praying" (Psalm 113:9, "He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother," would be the obvious scriptural match, and 1 Samuel 2 is Hannah's song). If Athanasius's letter names nothing like it, then 103 is the honest best, and it is a good one.
verdict.wouldHurt: Psalm 103 is printed in full. Verses 15-16 ("As for man, his days are like grass... when the wind passes over, it vanishes") could sting briefly for a woman early in a long-awaited pregnancy, who may fear miscarriage. The very next verse, 17 ("the loving devotion of the LORD extends from everlasting to everlasting... to children's children"), answers that fear well, so on the whole it comforts her. Nothing is misread. The fallback options about grinding down and fear would not fit her, but she never reaches them.
verdict.theirSituation: She is joyfully thanking God for a specific answered prayer, her pregnancy after two years of trying, and not giving thanks "through everything" in general.

results.desc: David, 35, Denver, Colorado, evangelical. He was promoted to regional manager, with a big raise and a team of twenty. He is thrilled and a bit wary of how much he wanted it, and he wants to stay humble and not let it take over his life.

answers.wanted: Something like "Thrilled, but wary of myself". None of the words gets at the worry that he wanted this too much and could let it swell his head. "Unsure" and "Anxious" point to fear about the outcome, and that isn't what he feels.
"Keep me humble" or "Don't let this go to my head". "Make me who You want me to be" is near, but it is about character in general, not the pull of success.

"Success at work, like a promotion" or "Something I worked hard for came through". He'd give God the credit, but every option reads the good as something spiritual, so there's nowhere to tap for a plain career win.

friction.note: The list has no word for mixed feelings about success or ambition, like wary, humbled or proud. Someone who is happy but watching his own heart gets flattened into plain happy.

The only follow-up about his own heart ("Something I keep going back to", "A sense that God is warning me") opens only through shame, guilt or feeling God is displeased. The quiet worry that ambition could take over his life never gets to show up, so the quiz may give him a simple thanksgiving psalm when he'd value a warning about pride.

"What's behind the good?" gives only faith-flavoured causes (leading, kindness, coming to faith, coming back). For a good that is really a job win, this feels like a nudge to spiritualise it. "A new home, or a new family" covers life events but not career. Adding "Something I worked for came through" would help.
"How great You are." and "Thank You." are fine, but no option names the "keep me grounded" prayer that many people pray in good times.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and easy for David. The core questions fit a good season well, but his main tension, being thrilled while wary of pride, had nowhere to go. He'd probably end up with a plain gratitude psalm and feel it missed the part he cared about most.

verdict.why: As David, I'd say yes to the first line. I'm an evangelical who just got the promotion I prayed about, so "the Lord shepherding you and guiding your way, and you're glad" is how I'd describe this season. It catches the thrilled, grateful half of me. Psalm 23 also turns out to fit better than the line suggests: "I shall not want" is a quiet check on a man who wanted this promotion a little too much, and "He leads me in paths of righteousness for His name's sake" reminds me whose name matters. But the line only speaks to the gladness. It says nothing about my real worry, which is staying humble and not letting a team of twenty and a big raise take over my life. Line 2, Psalm 15, is closer to that worry: honest dealing, no bribes, keeping your word even when it costs you. That's the psalm a new manager with power over people's pay should read. I only got there because I'd have tapped "Yes" on line 1 before reading line 2. The order puts comfort ahead of the thing I actually named. The fallback routes (grinding, weighing, afraid) would have been wrong for me: nothing is wearing me down, I'm doing well and a bit wary.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. The risk runs the other way: "the Lord is guiding you, rejoice" can read as a blessing on the promotion and a pat on the back, which feeds the pride I'm trying to watch. If the result page says nothing about "I shall not want" as a word against wanting more, a man in my spot could come away more pleased with himself, not more humble.
verdict.theirSituation: A new success he's thankful for, and a worry that ambition and pride will take over his life. It's a "good season, guard your heart" situation, not trouble.

results.desc: Mei, 26, Singapore, Presbyterian. Her best friend from university, who she had talked with about faith for years, was baptised on Sunday. Mei cried the whole way through and has felt light and hopeful all week.

answers.wanted: Something wonderful just happened. The list has 'Something hard just happened' but nothing for a sudden good thing. My best friend's baptism on Sunday is the reason for the good week.
My best friend's faith. That is both 'Someone I love' and 'God, and my faith', and I could only pick one.
They've just come to faith / been baptised. 'Doing well, and I'm thankful' feels too small for years of praying for her, and 'new in my life' is wrong because she has been my friend for years.

friction.note: All the sudden-event options are negative ('Something hard just happened', 'Something hard is finally over'). Someone whose week turned on one joyful event has to pick 'new' or 'better' as a stand-in.

'Someone I love' reads a bit romantic or family-shaped for a best friend. It would help if the question allowed picking two, like feel and people do, because her joy is about a friend and about faith together.

The 'loved' follow-up is mostly about suffering, illness, need or loss. The one happy option ('doing well') is generic, and the most natural joyful case for a Christian, a loved one coming to faith, is missing here, although it does show up later under 'good'.
This fitted perfectly, but it felt like I had half-answered it already in 'loved'. Asking about a friend's faith in two places might feel repetitive.

results.overall: This was quick and mostly pleasant. The joyful options (Hopeful, Grateful, A real gift, Clearly at work, Thank You) let Mei say exactly how she feels. The early questions lean toward hardship, though, so a person having one specific happy event has to pick approximations until the 'What's behind the good?' question finally names it.

verdict.why: Line 2 is exactly my week. I watched my friend be made new and I cried because God loves us that much. Line 1 is true in a vague way, since I do want to thank God. But "in and through everything" sounds like staying grateful when life is hard, not like the joy I feel right now. So I'd tap "Not quite", though I nearly said yes. That is a risk: a less patient person would stop at line 1 and never see the line that names her. The baptism line is much more specific and should probably come first for someone whose answers point to it. Psalm 32 fits. Its opening, "Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven", is what baptism means to me as a Presbyterian. Being told to "sing it over them" gives me something to do: I could pray it for her or send it to her. I'd feel seen, not boxed in.
verdict.theirSituation: She is overjoyed that a close friend she talked with about faith for years has just been baptised.

results.desc: Patrick, 78, Dublin, Ireland, Catholic. His health is decent for his age and the grandchildren were over all weekend. He is content, thinks about death now and then without fear, and feels God has been good to him over a long life.

answers.wanted: My family, the grandchildren. Or getting on in years and what comes after, which is on his mind now and then.
He's been good to me all my life. A long life, well blessed.

friction.note: There's no option for growing old or thinking about death. For a 78-year-old that's the most natural thing on his mind besides family. 'What's next for me' reads like a job or a move, not the end of life. 'Someone I love' is close, but it feels like it's asking about one person in trouble, not a houseful of grandchildren.

'What's behind the good?' is a bit awkward. None of the options looks back over a whole life. They're about new things: leading, growth, a new home, coming to faith. 'Everything, really' is a shrug, not gratitude for decades.
'They're doing well, and I'm thankful' fits. But the list is mostly trouble (suffering, danger, need, losing them), so a contented grandfather has to read past a run of bad news first.

results.overall: He'd get through it quickly and without trouble. Most questions have a plain, cheerful answer for a content old man. What's missing is anywhere to say he's old and at peace with death, and anywhere to be thankful for a long life rather than for something new.

verdict.why: Patrick is content and grateful after a long life, and he feels God has been good to him. "You want to thank God, in and through everything" is exactly how he feels, so he says yes at once. Psalm 103 fits him closely. It opens with "do not forget all His kind deeds", which suits a man looking back on many years. Later in the psalm come "man's days are like grass" and "from everlasting to everlasting His loving devotion", which meet his calm thoughts about death without making them heavy. Line 2 (Psalm 145) would also have fitted, so the ordering is right and neither line boxes him in.

results.desc: Milica, 49, Belgrade, Serbia, Orthodox. The fasting season she kept this summer went better than any before, and she feels clear-headed and calm. Work is steady and the family is well; she mostly wants to hold on to the quiet she found.

answers.wanted: Steady, and I want to keep it that way
Keeping the peace I've found
The fast went well and I feel clearer. Prayer and discipline, not me growing on my own

friction.note: Nothing for 'settled and steady'. 'About the same' sounds flat, not like a good calm she wants to keep.
'God, and my faith' is very broad. What is on her mind is holding on to a calm she found, and no option says that.

Nothing fits a good stretch that came from church life, like a fast or a feast season. 'I'm growing' sounds a little self-help to an Orthodox woman who would give the credit to God's mercy. 'A new home, or a new family' does not fit someone whose life is steady.
An Orthodox woman might reach for 'Lord, have mercy', and it is missing. 'Make me who You want me to be' reads a bit like an evangelical phrase to her.

results.overall: It was quick and felt mostly right. The quiz clearly has room for a calm, grateful person and 'Stay with me' fit her exactly. But nothing lets her say 'steady, and I want to keep it', and the good-times follow-up does not know what a church season like a fast is.

verdict.why: The only line offered is close to her. A fast that went better than any before is a real step up in how she lives, and the Songs of Ascents are a natural fit for an Orthodox woman who knows them from the eighteenth kathisma at Vespers, so she would tap yes. But the wording leans the wrong way. "Straining toward what's ahead" is effort and pushing. What she feels is calm, and she wants to keep a quiet she already has, not climb further. She would accept it as near enough and would probably read Psalm 121 gladly ("He who keeps you will not slumber" speaks directly to guarding something). Still, she would notice that nothing was written for peace she wants to keep. If she said "Not quite", the fallback would be worse: all three options assume something is grinding her down, weighing on her or frightening her. None of that is her, and it would make the quiz feel as if it only knows about trouble.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. The only risk is small: "straining" and "climbing" could make her feel pushed to do more when she is content, as if her calm were just a stop on the way up.
verdict.theirSituation: She is at peace after a good fast, and what she wants is to hold on to that quiet and guard it, not to strain forward or get through any trouble.

results.desc: Jorge, 44, Bogotá, Colombia, evangelical. A former business partner who cheated him lost the court case this month, and Jorge's small printing business has finally paid off its debts. He feels vindicated and relieved, and grateful that he didn't take matters into his own hands.

answers.wanted: Relieved, or vindicated. Grateful fits, but 'At peace' is only an approximation of relief.
The court case with my old partner, and the business finally being out of debt. Only one choice is allowed, so the money and work side is lost.
One person cheated me, but that's settled now, and everyone else has been kind. The options only describe the present, so the partner who turned on him drops out.
One person who cheated me. 'People who were against me' is plural, and 'A falling-out' is too mild for fraud and a court case.

friction.note: It only asks about now ('lately'), so someone whose conflict just ended has no way to say one person turned on him but it's over. He has to choose between 'One person has turned on me', which is no longer true, and 'Kind to me', which leaves the story out.
There's no 'Relieved' option, and relief is the main feeling when something hard is over. 'At peace' is close but not the same thing.
'People who were against me' is plural. Being cheated by a single business partner fits it only loosely. 'Someone who wronged me' would fit better.
You can pick only one here, but his mind is on both the person (the lawsuit) and money/work (debts paid off). One pick loses half the picture.
This follow-up is skipped when trend is 'over', even though he feels good. That's probably intended, but he never gets to say that the business paying off its debts is part of the good.

results.overall: It was quick and felt natural. 'Something hard is finally over', 'I left it with Him, and He set it right' and 'Thank You' fit Jorge exactly, and he'd feel understood. The only friction was around the person who wronged him: the present-tense people question and the plural 'people who were against me' made him bend the story a little.

verdict.why: As Jorge I'd hesitate at line 1. "People were hunting you" sounds like my life was in danger. My partner cheated me and I fought him in court; nobody hunted me. Psalm 18 also has David chasing down his enemies and crushing them "fine as dust", and that clashes with what I'm most grateful for: I didn't take revenge, God settled it. So I'd say "Not quite". Line 2, wanting to thank God in and through everything, is where my heart is this month: the debts are paid, the case is closed, and I'm thankful. Psalm 103 fits me well. It names forgiveness, rescue "from the pit", and 103:6, "The LORD executes righteousness and justice for all the oppressed", which covers the court case without making me gloat. I'd feel seen, and I'd want to read it.
verdict.theirSituation: He was wronged by someone close, and God vindicated him through a fair court and a business finally out of debt, so he feels relieved and justified and is grateful he waited on God instead of taking revenge.

results.desc: Abigail, 21, Cape Town, South Africa, Anglican. University is going well, she has a new boyfriend she really likes, and she has good friends around her. She's busy and happy and thanks God often, though mostly on the run.

answers.wanted: Getting better. Things were already good and a new relationship has started, so it is not quite one new thing starting
My new boyfriend. 'Someone I love' feels too strong this early, so 'People in my life' is the nearest
Something like 'Good, I thank Him a lot but on the go'. 'Close' flatters it a bit, and 'Just there, in the background' sells it short
'Good people around me: friends, and someone new.' 'A new home, or a new family' almost fits, but a boyfriend isn't family

friction.note: There is no option for a new relationship or romance. 'Someone I love' is too heavy for a few weeks in, and the follow-up for it ('They're suffering…', 'I'm losing them') is mostly about bad news.
The options run from far to close, but none fits a happy person who thanks God often in passing. 'Close' feels like overclaiming, and 'in the background' feels like admitting to drifting.

'Coming to faith', 'Coming back to Him' and 'I can see Him leading me' feel tilted toward a spiritual answer. For an ordinary good patch (uni, friends, boyfriend) the only real choice is 'Everything, really', which is vague.
'Something new is starting' and 'Getting better' overlap when life is good and a relationship has just begun. It's unclear which one is meant.

results.overall: It was quick and pleasant, and most of it fitted a happy, busy student. But the quiz seems built for hard times: the good path is thin, it has no word for a new relationship, and the God question made her pick a slightly more pious answer than she'd honestly give.

verdict.why: Abigail is happy, grateful, and thanks God often. "You want to thank God, in and through everything" is the first line and fits her at once. Psalm 103:2, "do not forget all His kind deeds", speaks straight to someone whose thanks are real but rushed. It gently asks her to slow down and count what she has, which rings true without scolding. Athanasius's note that you can "stir up your own soul" also suits someone who thanks God on the run. "In and through everything" sounds a little weightier than her light, busy life, since it hints at thanking God through hardship too. That is a small stretch, and she would still say yes.

results.desc: Frank, 71, Naples, Florida, Presbyterian. Retired and comfortable, he plays golf twice a week and volunteers at a food pantry. Life is good, and sometimes he wonders whether it's a bit too easy and what God might still want from him.

answers.wanted: Grateful, and a bit comfortable, maybe too comfortable. 'Restless' is stronger than what he feels. He'd want something like 'Wondering' or 'Too comfortable'.
What God still wants from me. That falls between 'What's next for me' and 'God, and my faith'. He'd have tapped both if he could.
Good to me, but I wonder whether I've got too comfortable with Him. 'Background' is fair but sounds a little harsher than he'd say it.
I've been blessed, more than I deserve. He'd also nearly tap 'His kindness, to me and to everyone'.

friction.note: Nothing fits a man who is content but has a slightly guilty feeling that life is too easy. 'Restless' makes it sound like a problem. Most of the list is about distress, so a comfortable person has to pick 'Grateful' plus something that overstates the unease.
'What's next for me' sounds like a career or a move to a retiree. His real question is 'what does God still want from me?', and it is split across two options.
There is no option for 'close, but I may have got complacent'. 'Just there, in the background' can feel like admitting a lukewarm faith, a bit of a box for a steady Presbyterian.
Half the options are about being attacked or mocked. For a contented retiree they read as heavy, but they're easy to skip past.
'Coming back to Him' and 'A new home, or a new family' don't apply to most older, settled people. 'Everything, really' is a little vague but works.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy for him to answer. But the quiz clearly leans toward people in trouble, so a comfortable, grateful man who quietly wonders whether life is too easy had to stretch to 'restless' and 'background' to show his mild unease.

verdict.why: Frank would say yes to line 1, though with a small wince. He isn't lapsed: he gives his time at the food pantry and goes to church. But his real worry is that an easy life has made him comfortable and drowsy toward God, and "wake your soul up to Him" names that honestly. Psalm 103 fits a blessed retiree very well. "Do not forget all His kind deeds" is a call to gratitude for someone who has a lot. Its lines on man's days being like grass also land at 71. Athanasius's "give thanks through everything" is a gentle way in, not a scolding. The one gap is his other question, "what might God still want from me?" Psalm 103 doesn't answer it. Line 2 (Psalm 15, what kind of person dwells with God) answers it better. He might have preferred that line, but he would stop at line 1 first. Line 3 does not fit him at all, since nothing is weighing on him.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Slipped into the background" could read as a mild charge of backsliding against a man who serves every week. It's close enough that he won't take offence, but a phrase like "life is easy and your soul has gone quiet" would describe him more accurately.
verdict.theirSituation: Frank has a comfortable, blessed retirement and a faith he actively lives out, and he quietly wonders whether it has all become too easy and what God still asks of him.

results.desc: Nkechi, 39, London, UK, Nigerian Catholic. She had surgery for a lump in the summer and the results came back clear last week. She has been thankful every morning since and is trying to take less for granted.

answers.wanted: Something like 'Being thankful for what I have' - my health is on my mind, but as relief and thanks, not worry
'I prayed, and He answered, through the doctors' - I prayed and the results came back clear; 'He got me out' was nearly as right

friction.note: 'My health' reads as something worrying. Nothing lets her say that what's on her mind is gratitude for being well, or trying not to take things for granted.

She never got the 'What's behind the good?' question because her trend was 'Something hard is finally over'. She would have liked to answer it ('Everything, really' or 'An answered prayer'). Her feeling of taking less for granted has nowhere to go.

Nearly every option says God acted in a particular way. For a medical scare, the only other choice is 'It just passed', which feels too flat for a believer. That's fine for her, but an option like 'I prayed, and it came out well' would be gentler for someone who isn't sure what God did.
Picking 'A real gift' next to 'Against me' on the same list feels a little odd, but it's clear.

results.overall: Quick and easy for her, and 'Something hard is finally over' followed by 'An illness, or a scare' felt like it really understood her summer. The only thing that felt thin was that she couldn't say her gratitude is also about learning to take less for granted.

verdict.why: Every morning since the clear results, Nkechi has been thanking God and trying not to take things for granted. "You want to thank God, in and through everything" is her, and she would say yes at once. Psalm 103:2 ("do not forget all His kind deeds") matches her wish to take less for granted almost word for word. Once she reads the whole psalm she reaches 103:3-4, "who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the pit", which will feel written for her after the surgery. As a Catholic she will likely know it from the liturgy, and she would feel seen. One small point: line 2 ("He brought you through, and you want to tell people") is actually the more specific picture of her story. Some people in her place might pause on line 1 because it feels general. They would still take it, because it is true and it comes first. Nothing on either line misreads or hurts her. The fallback about grinding, weight and fear would never be reached, and it would have been wrong for someone whose news was good.

results.desc: Kenji, 53, Osaka, Japan, member of a small evangelical church. He and a colleague who had been cold to him for a year finally talked it through over dinner and made peace. It's a small thing, but he feels a quiet joy and sees God's hand in it.

answers.wanted: Quiet, but good. A small good thing happened. 'Good' feels a bit big and 'Quiet and ordinary' leaves out the joy.
Something that was wrong has been put right. A cold year with a colleague was hard, but 'something hard' sounds bigger than it was for him.
Someone who was cold to me has become warm again. The list has options for things going wrong and for things being good, but nothing for a relationship that has just been mended.

friction.note: 'Something hard is finally over' feels heavy for a small, everyday reconciliation. A modest person might hesitate and tap 'Getting better' instead, which would skip the 'What was it?' and 'How did it end?' questions that fit him best.
The steps from 'Quiet and ordinary' to 'Good' to 'Really good' are about how much. None fits 'a small but real joy', so a humble person has to pick between making it smaller or bigger than it feels.

The 'What's behind the good?' question is not asked when the answer to 'lately' is 'Something hard is finally over', even when he picked Grateful. 'I can see Him leading me' or 'His kindness' would have fitted him well here. The condition leaves out the thankful-after-trouble person.

Most options say God did it ('He got me out', 'He set it right'). 'We made peace' fits, but he sees God's hand in the peace too. An option like 'We made peace, and I see Him in it' would fit better. As it stands he has to choose between the human side and the God side.

'A real gift' and 'Kind to me' are close, but you cannot say 'someone who was cold is now warm'. For a non-native English reader, 'Upset with me, and with reason' and 'Hard to be around' are fine, but 'Far away, or gone' may be read as a comment on distance.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly easy. The feelings, God and 'Thank You' questions fitted him exactly, and the 'falling-out' and 'We made peace' follow-ups felt as if they were written for him. The main strain was the size of the words: his joy is small and quiet, and a few options asked him to call it bigger (or the past trouble harder) than it felt.

verdict.why: As Kenji, I would say yes to the first line. What I feel is quiet thankfulness: God softened a year of coldness, and I want to bless Him for it. "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds" is what I would want to say walking home from that dinner. The rest of Psalm 103 fits even better than the opening line. It speaks of God being slow to anger, of Him not always accusing, and of Him removing our wrongs as far as the east is from the west. Those are words about peace after a quarrel. The one small gap is "in and through everything". It sounds a bit big for a small, particular mercy. I am not feeling thankful for everything right now; I am thankful for this one thing. Still, it is close enough that I would not feel boxed in. Nothing here would wound me, and I would read the psalm through.
verdict.theirSituation: He is quietly thankful to God for one small, particular mercy: a year-long coldness with a colleague ended in reconciliation over dinner.

results.desc: Leah, 31, Portland, Oregon, returning after years away from church. After drifting through her twenties she has found a small church where she feels at home and has been going for four months. She feels welcomed, a little surprised at herself, and closer to God than she has in a long time.

answers.wanted: Something between 'Getting better' and 'Something new is starting'. Church began four months ago, so it is no longer brand new, but it still feels like a fresh start.
'I've found new people who welcome me' or 'A new community'. 'Kind to me' is right, but it misses that these people are new in her life.

friction.note: 'Getting better' and 'Something new is starting' both fit someone a few months into a new chapter. She would hesitate, because nothing says how recent 'new' has to be.
There is no word for being pleasantly surprised at herself, or for feeling welcomed. Grateful and Hopeful come close, so this is minor.
'Displeased with me' could land hard for someone coming back after years away, since it touches old church-guilt fears. She would not pick it, but seeing it offered might sting a little.

'Coming back to Him' fitted so exactly that it felt like being seen, which is good. 'A new home, or a new family' could also pull at someone who has found a church family. It might be worth making clear that church community counts there, or giving it its own option.

results.overall: It felt quick and warm, and nothing forced her into a box. The follow-up 'Coming back to Him' named her situation exactly, so she would be curious to see the psalm. The only small snags were deciding between 'better' and 'new', and having no option that says the kind people are new in her life.

verdict.why: Leah's main feeling right now is gratitude, and she is a little surprised to be back. "You want to thank God" fits her. Psalm 103 fits even better than the line suggests. "Do not forget all His kind deeds" matches someone looking back over years away. Later verses in the psalm, about forgiveness and a life redeemed from the pit, speak straight to a returner. She would say yes to the first line. The second line, about judgment mixed with mercy, doesn't fit her. She hasn't come through a judgment. She has been welcomed.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing would wound her. One small misread: "in and through everything" hints that she is thanking God in spite of hardship, but her season is simply good. The line also says nothing about coming home after years away, which is the heart of her story, so she recognises herself mostly because of the psalm's text and less because of the line.
verdict.theirSituation: She is thankful, and surprised to be close to God again after years away, and she has found a church that feels like home.

results.desc: Dana, 44, Columbus, Ohio, Methodist. Her divorce was finalised in August, and her ex-husband has been telling their friends and his family that she had an affair, which isn't true. She is angry most days and is trying hard not to say anything bad about him in front of their two kids. God feels like someone watching from a distance who hasn't stepped in.

answers.wanted: Something like 'It's over, but it isn't': the divorce is final, but the lies he's telling keep going
'Watching, but not stepping in': He feels like He's there and sees it, but isn't doing anything
'My ex, or a former partner'. It's one person, my ex-husband, telling our friends and his family. 'Family, or the people closest to me' was the nearest, but he isn't really family any more

friction.note: She had already tapped 'One person has turned on me', and then she's asked 'Who are they, mostly?', which is plural and assumes a group. She would want to say it's one person (her ex) with an audience (friends, his family). There's no option for an ex or a former spouse, which is a very common case for this question.

There's nothing in between 'Far away' and 'Silent'. What she feels is that God sees it and is choosing not to step in. 'Far away' makes Him sound absent, when her complaint is that He's present and not acting.

She can't say 'it's finished on paper but still going'. 'Something hard is finally over' would be half true (the divorce is final) but would open questions about how it ended, which would be wrong for her.

There's no way to say the people around her are split: some believe the lie and some are kind to her. She could have picked 'Kind to me' as well, but the one-or-two limit pushed her toward the hurt side.
There's no word for holding it in or biting her tongue, which is a big part of her days (not running him down in front of the kids). Angry and Hurt cover it well enough.

results.overall: It felt quick, and closer to her life than she expected. 'Clear my name.' and 'What they're saying about me' hit hard and felt seen. The follow-up asking 'who are they' felt slightly off when it's really one person, her ex. God being 'far away' was near her feeling but not quite it.

verdict.why: He is telling people I had an affair, and I didn't.
