"They won't stop trying to ruin you" is what that feels like, and "you want someone to finally judge who's in the right" is the exact ache: our friends and his family are ruling on my marriage from his side of the story. I'd tap "Yes, that's it." Psalm 26 opens "Vindicate me, O LORD! For I have walked with integrity." That's what I'd pray if I had the words. The advice is the part that really lands: don't let any human verdict be the last word, because everything human is open to doubt, and let God be the Judge. That gives me somewhere to put the anger, so I don't have to argue my case to everyone or say it in front of the kids. "My feet stand on level ground" is a steadying place to end, and the pointer to Psalm 35 fits too, since it's about false witnesses. What it misses is the feeling that God is watching from a distance and hasn't stepped in. The psalm assumes God will judge, and part of me doubts He's even paying attention. Line 2 was close too, but "more and more rising up" is too big for what I'm living. It's one man and the people he's convinced.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. One small risk: the full text of Psalm 26 has lines like "I wash my hands in innocence" and "I do not sit with deceitful men". On an angry day those could read as permission to feel righteous against him rather than to hand the verdict over. The advice's framing, that God is the Judge and not me, prevents that, so it should stay prominent. The result also doesn't touch the feeling that God is distant.
verdict.theirSituation: A recently divorced mother is being falsely accused of an affair by her ex among their friends and his family. She is angry, holding her tongue for the kids, and feels God is distant.

results.desc: Chinedu, 29, Lagos, Nigeria, Pentecostal. A colleague moved money wrongly at the bank where they both work and arranged the records so it looks like Chinedu did it. He has been suspended during the inquiry and his manager won't meet his eye. He prays every night for the truth to come out, but part of him is afraid it won't.

answers.wanted: Stuck waiting for an outcome (the inquiry hasn't decided yet)
Believing a lie about me / blaming me for something I didn't do
Near, and I'm waiting on Him to act
Both a colleague and the people with power over me (my manager); could only pick one
Being blamed for something I didn't do, and that the lie might stick

friction.note: No option for being falsely accused or wrongly blamed. 'Talking about me' sounds like gossip, and 'Against me' sounds like open hostility. Neither quite fits a manager who quietly believes a set-up.
There's no 'waiting for an outcome' (an inquiry, a diagnosis, a verdict). 'About the same' makes it sound calmer than it feels.
It's single-pick, but the colleague who framed me and the boss who believes it are two different groups. A second tap would help.

'What they might be planning' and 'Not knowing what they'll do next' sound like being hunted. The real fear is the unfair verdict: losing my job and my name over a lie. There's nothing like 'The truth not coming out'.
Nothing for 'wronged' or 'falsely accused'. 'Hurt' was the nearest.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy, and 'Clear my name.' felt like it was written for me, so that part hit home. The people and hardest-part questions assume I'm being bullied or gossiped about rather than set up and falsely blamed, so I had to choose the nearest options there.

verdict.why: Line 1 is the only one about being wronged by someone and wanting a true judgment, and that is exactly Chinedu's prayer every night. Psalm 26:1, "Vindicate me, O LORD! For I have walked with integrity", is close to word for word what he would say about the framing. The psalm also has lines against sitting with deceitful men, which fits a colleague who doctored the records. Athanasius's advice not to let any human verdict be the last word speaks straight to his fear that the bank's inquiry will get it wrong. It gives him somewhere to stand even if the truth does not come out. The turn at 26:12, "my feet stand on level ground", reads like the hope of being cleared and back among people who trust him. Lines 2 and 3 touch on his fear and unease, but they would feel generic next to this one.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. There is a small misfit in the wording. "They won't stop trying to ruin you" pictures an ongoing campaign by enemies, but his case is one colleague's single betrayal and its fallout: he is suspended, under investigation, and his manager avoids him. The line also never says "falsely accused" or "blamed for something you didn't do", which is the heart of it for him, so he might hesitate a moment before tapping yes. The advice's line that "everything human is open to doubt" is comforting, but it could briefly read as saying the inquiry doesn't matter, when he is hoping it finds the truth.
verdict.theirSituation: A colleague framed him for moving money wrongly, and he has been suspended while an inquiry runs. He prays for the truth to come out and is afraid it won't.

results.desc: Martin, 52, Manchester, UK, lapsed Catholic. He had three years sober and started drinking again three weeks ago after his brother's funeral. He hasn't told his sponsor or his wife and feels like a fraud at his AA meetings. He isn't sure God would want to hear from him right now.

answers.wanted: Both at once: something hard happened (the funeral) and it has got worse since (the drinking). I tapped 'Getting worse' because the drinking is the live part.
Two things tied together: my brother, and what I've done since. I'd have liked to pick 'Someone or something I've lost' as well as 'Something I've done'.
'They don't know what's really going on with me.' My wife and my sponsor are kind because I'm hiding it, and my brother is gone.
'I don't think He'd want to hear from me.' It sits between 'Displeased with me' and 'I've drifted from Him'.

friction.note: Every option describes how people treat me. None covers them not knowing, which is the whole situation for someone hiding a relapse or an affair. 'Kind to me' fits but hurts to tap, because they are only kind because they don't know.
Only one pick here, but grief and what he did after it are one knot. Being made to choose between 'Someone or something I've lost' and 'Something I've done' feels like being put in a box.

'Displeased with me' is close, but what he feels is that he isn't worth listening to right now. That is shame, not God's anger. A lapsed Catholic could read 'Displeased' as the stern God he walked away from.
'A sense that God is warning me' sounds a bit preachy next to the others. 'Something I keep going back to' is very good: he can admit the drinking without the quiz naming it.
'Something hard just happened' and 'Getting worse' are both true (the loss, then the spiral), and he can only pick one.

results.overall: It felt quick and surprisingly gentle. He could say 'ashamed', 'sorry' and 'something I keep going back to' without the quiz ever saying 'addiction'. The one miss is the people question: it has no way to say 'they don't know', which is the fraud feeling at the heart of his situation.

verdict.why: As Martin, I would stop at the first line. I'm ashamed, I've been hiding it, and part of me wants to come back. Psalm 51 opens with "according to Your great compassion", which answers the question I'm actually carrying: would God even want to hear from me? The turn to "wash me, and I will be whiter than snow" is the kind of hope a relapsed man needs. Line 2 (a warning shaking me) would feel off, and line 3 is true but too vague. Line 1 fits the relapse and the hiding. It says nothing about the grief behind them, my brother's death.
verdict.wouldHurt: The bare "You have sinned" in Athanasius's advice is the risky part. Someone in AA has learned to see relapse as part of an illness, not a moral failure, and in the first seconds this line could read as a verdict that feeds the shame that is keeping me drinking and keeping me quiet. The result also sees only the wrongdoing, not the grief that set it off. And "you want to come back" assumes a readiness I'm not sure I have. My question is whether I'm allowed back. If the page led with mercy, or gently named the grief, it would land more softly. For results reached this way, a quiet line pointing to real people would matter: a sponsor, a priest, or a helpline (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK, since 988 is US-only).
verdict.theirSituation: A grieving man who relapsed after three years sober and is hiding it. He is ashamed and unsure God or his AA group would still have him, so repentance fits, but grief is what's underneath it.

results.desc: Ji-won, 36, Seoul, South Korea, Presbyterian. Last week she found out their third round of IVF failed, and two women in her small group have just announced pregnancies. She smiles at church and cries in the car afterwards. She still prays but feels God has gone quiet on the one thing she keeps asking for.

answers.wanted: Grieving, or 'heartbroken'. 'Sad' is too small for losing a hoped-for child, and 'Hurt' makes it sound like someone did it to her.
Something I long for that isn't happening (a child). 'Someone or something I've lost' is nearest, but she never had the baby, so it feels odd to call it a loss. 'My health' is wrong too.
Their good news is hard for me, though it isn't their fault. 'Hard to be around' makes the pregnant friends sound like the problem, and she would feel guilty tapping it.

friction.note: There is no option for longing or waiting for something that has not come, such as a child, a spouse or healing. Infertility has to squeeze into 'lost', which does not fit, or 'My health', which feels clinical. A woman in her situation may feel the quiz was not written for her.

'Hard to be around' reads as blaming the person. She loves these women and is happy for them. She needs something like 'Their joy is hard for me right now' so she can answer honestly without accusing anyone.
'Sad' is fine but light for grief. A word like 'Grieving' or 'Heartbroken' would let her feel seen. No other wording felt preachy.

'Something hard just happened' fits, but a failed IVF round is also part of a long pattern. If there were a 'long wait' route for people who are still in the middle of it, she would want it here, not only under 'Something hard is finally over'.

results.overall: For a grieving woman it was quick and mostly gentle. 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside', 'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' and 'How long?' felt as if they were written about her. But no option names the thing she actually carries, an unanswered longing for a child, and the only way to say the pregnant friends are hard for her makes her sound like she blames them.

verdict.why: As Ji-won I would tap "Yes, that's it" on line 1. It isn't exact, but it's close enough. "Weighed down... and it won't settle" fits the grief that keeps coming back every time I ask again and hear nothing. Psalm 42 is a good match once I read it in full. Tears have been my food day and night (42:3). I remember going with the crowd to the house of God with shouts of joy while grieving inside (42:4), which is me smiling at church and crying in the car. "Why have You forgotten me?" (42:9) is how God's silence feels. Other people saying "Where is your God?" is how the pregnancy announcements feel. It never mentions infertility, so it doesn't box me in. It gives me words for the ache and the silence and leaves the cause to me. I'd feel seen, not diagnosed.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Uneasy" is too mild a word for grief over a third failed IVF round. "Weighed down" carries the line, and "uneasy" makes it sound like anxiety. The Athanasius advice ("what grieves you is healed") could read as a promise of a quick fix, or a hint that singing should make it go away. That would sting when God has stayed quiet on the one thing I keep asking for. Both verses shown (42:5 and 42:11) are the "put your hope in God" refrain. Shown alone, they risk sounding like "cheer up and have more faith", which is exactly what I pretend to do at church. Putting 42:3 or 42:9 (tears as food, "Why have You forgotten me?") near the top would show that the psalm lets me grieve before it asks me to hope.
verdict.theirSituation: She is grieving a third failed IVF round and God's silence on her one prayer, while hiding the grief behind a smile at church around friends who have just announced pregnancies.

results.desc: Guadalupe, 67, Mexico City, Catholic. Her mother has dementia and lives with her. Some nights her mother doesn't recognise her and gets frightened and angry. Guadalupe is worn out, feels guilty for sometimes wishing it were over, and hasn't been to Mass in two months because she can't leave the house.

answers.wanted: Getting worse, slowly, and it won't get better. With dementia it isn't a stretch that ends. "About the same" was nearly as true.
Worn out and Guilty. What she feels is guilt for wishing it were over. "Ashamed" is heavier and sounds like she did something disgraceful.
"The person I care for doesn't know me" and "I'm alone with it". "Hard to be around" is true of her mother's bad nights, but it feels disloyal to tap it about a sick mother.
"I can't get to Him the way I used to". She hasn't missed Mass by choice. "I've drifted" would sound like it's her fault, and "far away" is only close.

friction.note: There is no "Guilty" option. A carer's guilt is not shame, so "Ashamed" is the nearest but it feels like it accuses her of something worse than she did.

Every option describes people as a group, and several are about enemies (against me, mocking, talking). No option fits caring for a sick person who is frightened and angry at you. "Hard to be around" makes her mother sound like a difficult person rather than an ill one.
"I've drifted from Him" makes missing Mass sound like a choice. She misses it because she can't leave the house. Nothing covers "I can't get to church" or "I'm cut off from the sacraments".

The heading "Which is closest?" is vague: closest to what? "A sense that God is warning me" could frighten someone who is already guilty and worn out. "Where my thoughts have taken me" fits, but it's a bit oblique for a quick tap.

"I'm losing them" fits dementia well. The quiz then treats her as losing someone, when it is really an ongoing grief while her mother is still alive. Nowhere does it ask about being the one who does the caring.
The options expect a story that moves (worse, better, over, new). Long caregiving is a grinding sameness that is still getting worse, and no option describes it.

results.overall: For her, most answers were quick and honest ("Really hard", "Someone I love", "I'm so tired", "I'm losing them"). She would feel mildly boxed in because the quiz has no words for a carer's guilt or for being kept from church by circumstance, and some options for her mother read as if her mother were an adversary.

verdict.why: "Worn down until you feel empty and listless, and you need comfort" is how I feel most nights, so I would tap "Yes, that's it" straight away. Psalm 102 fits better than I expected. "I even forget to eat my bread" is exactly me, feeding my mother and forgetting myself. Later in the psalm, the lonely sparrow on the housetop and the "days like a shadow" feel like my nights awake with her. The turn in verse 17, that God will not despise the prayer of the destitute, is what I need, because I haven't been able to get to Mass and I half fear He has stopped listening. It doesn't name my guilt or my mother, but it doesn't have to. It meets me in the tiredness, and it's a prayer I can say at home. I'm glad I stopped at line 1. Line 2, "wrong thoughts carried you off... and you're sorry", might have caught me on a guilty night and made my wish that it were over feel like a sin I'm being told to weep over.
verdict.wouldHurt: Almost nothing in Psalm 102 would hurt me. "Our nature is weak" feels kind, not like a scolding. Two small things. "Poor" in Athanasius's advice might make me think it means money. At 67, with my mother fading, the lines about my days being cut short ("do not take me away in the midst of my days") hit hard, even though they're true. The real risk is line 2. For a caregiver who feels guilty, "wrong thoughts... you're sorry" could read as a verdict on her. If someone like me tapped "Not quite" on line 1 and reached it, it could wound.
verdict.theirSituation: A worn-out 67-year-old looking after her mother, who has dementia, at home. She feels guilty for sometimes wishing it were over and hasn't been able to get to Mass. Line 1 names the exhaustion but not the caregiving or the guilt.

results.desc: Nikos, 71, Chicago, Greek Orthodox. His wife died four months ago after 46 years of marriage. The house is very quiet, he eats standing up, and the people who brought food have stopped coming. He lights a candle for her every Sunday but mostly feels numb.

answers.wanted: Something hard happened a few months ago and it hasn't let up. "Just happened" is too recent and "about the same" sounds like nothing happened.
They were kind at first, but they've stopped coming. "Far away, or gone" reads oddly when the person who is gone is my wife.
I don't feel anything. I keep going to church and lighting the candle, but it's all numb.
Remember her. Give her rest. As an Orthodox man, praying for her is what I actually say to Him every Sunday, and there's no option for it.

friction.note: "Far away, or gone" is ambiguous for a widower. Is "gone" about friends drifting off or about the dead? There's no option for people who were kind and have now stopped coming, which is the most common experience a few months after a funeral.
"Someone or something I've lost" puts his wife of 46 years next to "something". That's a small sting. It still fits, but a separate "Someone who died" option would feel more respectful.

There's no numb option. Everything assumes you feel God one way or another. "Silent. I pray and nothing changes" doesn't fit either, because nothing can change: she is dead. That wording assumes a request is waiting to be answered.

There's nothing about praying for the dead ("Remember her", "Give her rest"). For a Greek Orthodox widower that is the most natural thing to say to God. The list reads as written for someone praying only about their own trouble.
No option fits a loss from a few months ago that still dominates everything. "Something hard just happened" feels too recent, and "About the same" plays it down.
There's "Sad" but no "Grieving". For a bereaved person, "Sad" feels too small.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and mostly easy for him to answer, and choosing \"Numb\" and \"Someone or something I've lost\" made him feel seen. But none of the questions directly names bereavement, God feeling numb, or praying for his wife. As a grieving Orthodox widower he had to settle for near-misses on four of the seven questions.

verdict.why: Nikos is numb, not anxious. "Empty and listless" is the closest thing to what he feels. The shown verse, "I even forget to eat my bread", hits him hard, because he eats standing up or not at all. Line 2 ("uneasy, won't settle") describes agitation he doesn't have. He would tap yes on line 1 because the verse lands, not because the line names his life. "Life has worn you down" makes it sound like he's been through a hard stretch. What actually happened is that his wife died, and the wording treats that like any other hard stretch. Psalm 102 in full also has the lonely sparrow on the housetop and "my days are like a shadow". A widower of 71 alone in a quiet house would feel those lines were written for him. So the result would speak to him, even though the question never asked about her.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. Two small misreads. First, Athanasius's line "the pressures of life... leave you feeling poor" frames his loss as ordinary wear and stress, which quietly shrinks a death into a busy season. Second, as a Greek Orthodox man his prayer book uses Septuagint numbering, where this psalm is 101. Seeing only "Psalm 102" could confuse him when he looks for it at church. Showing "(101 in Orthodox books)" would make him feel the site knows his tradition.
verdict.theirSituation: A widower four months into grief after 46 years of marriage. He is numb and alone, he has stopped eating proper meals, and the support has faded. It isn't that life has worn him down; he has lost her.

results.desc: Wanjiru, 19, Nairobi, Kenya, Anglican. In her first year at university she was diagnosed with Crohn's disease, and she has missed so many lectures that she might have to repeat the year. She is scared about what the rest of her life will look like and embarrassed to explain it to friends. She keeps asking God why now.

answers.wanted: Afraid and Embarrassed. 'Ashamed' sounds like I did something wrong, but I only picked it because nothing else is close to embarrassed about being sick.
My health, though it's really my health and school and my future all at once; I'd have liked to pick two here
They don't really know what's going on with me / I've been hiding it from them
Somewhere between 'Silent' and 'Far away'. I don't doubt He's there, I just don't understand why He let this happen
None of these. I haven't done anything wrong, I'm embarrassed about being ill. I'd want 'It's not something I did, I'm just embarrassed' or a way to skip this

friction.note: There's no 'Embarrassed'. Picking 'Ashamed' as the nearest word turns her illness into a question about her sin in the next step, which would hurt someone with a stigmatised illness.

This follow-up comes up because she tapped 'Ashamed', and every option assumes wrongdoing ('Something I did', 'Something I keep going back to', 'God is warning me'). For someone whose shame is about her body, this is a box, and 'A sense that God is warning me' could read as 'your Crohn's is a punishment'. That would be painful and would sound preachy. It needs a 'Not something I did' option, or it should not fire only on 'ashamed'.
Only one pick, while health, school and the future are tangled together for her. 'What's next for me' and 'Work or school' pull just as hard as 'My health'.
No option for 'they don't know' or 'I've been hiding it'. The options describe how people treat her, but her problem is that she hasn't told them.

'Silent. I pray and nothing changes' is close, but with a chronic illness 'nothing changes' feels heavy. There's no plain 'I don't understand what He's doing' option, even though her 'Why?' is exactly that.

results.overall: The core questions were quick and mostly felt like they understood her: really hard, getting worse, my health, 'Why?'. The shame follow-up would jar her, though. It reads as if the quiz thinks her illness is her own fault, and it could put her off the result.

verdict.why: Line 1 is not me at all. I haven't been carried off by wrong thoughts, I've been carried off by my body. Reading it while I keep asking God "why now" feels a little like being told this is my fault. Line 2 is the first one I would say yes to. I am afraid, about the rest of my life, about repeating the year, about what I'll tell my friends, and I do need something to hold on to. "The LORD is my strength and my song" is a line I could keep with me in hospital. But it only half fits. "What can man do to me?" is about fearing people, and I'm not afraid of people, I'm afraid of a disease with no end date. Nothing picks up the "why now" or the shame of explaining it to friends. Psalm 102 ("It's grinding me down") or Psalm 42 ("It's weighing on me, and it won't lift") from the fallback might actually be closer to me, but I would never reach them, because I would stop at line 2.
verdict.wouldHurt: Psalm 118 is printed in full, and 118:18 says "The LORD has chastened me severely". For a newly diagnosed teenager asking "why now", that can read as "your illness is God punishing you", unless something quiet frames it or the turn at 118:17 ("I shall not die, but live") is what gets emphasised. Line 1's "wrong thoughts... you're sorry" also feels a little accusatory when it's the first thing shown to someone whose trouble is illness, not sin.
verdict.theirSituation: A 19-year-old newly diagnosed with Crohn's disease who is afraid of a future with a chronic illness, ashamed to explain it to friends, and asking God why this happened now.

results.desc: Marcus, 38, Atlanta, Georgia, non-denominational. It's a busy month but a fine one: he has two kids under eight, a product launch at work, and a hockey schedule to juggle. He dropped his Bible reading plan somewhere around week three. God feels like background music, there but not really listened to.

answers.wanted: Something like 'Stretched' or 'Distracted'. He isn't really worn out, just spread thin, and the good things are there but he isn't feeling them much.
Something like 'Sorry I've been so distracted' or 'I'll get back to You'. That is a sheepish, light apology for drifting, not the heavy guilt 'I'm sorry.' suggests.
'My family and my life are full': kids, work going well, a good busy life. None of the options name ordinary blessings like family or work, and 'A new home, or a new family' is about something new.

friction.note: There is no word for the most common state of a busy, fine life: stretched thin, distracted or scattered. 'Worn out' overstates it and 'Restless' means something else.

Most of the fourteen options are crisis or lament lines ('How long?', 'Why?', 'Clear my name.', 'It isn't fair.'). Someone who is fine but has drifted has nothing that fits between 'I'm sorry.' (too heavy) and 'Thank You.' (too tidy). Scrolling past all the hard ones can make a person in a fine season feel the quiz isn't meant for them.

'What's behind the good?' is a slightly odd way to ask. The options lean spiritual ('I can see Him leading me', 'Coming back to Him'). There is nothing for everyday blessings like kids, a job going well or health, so 'Everything, really' becomes the catch-all.
'Just there, in the background' fits well and doesn't feel like a judgment. Good wording, keep it.

results.overall: For Marcus the quiz went quickly and mostly felt like it saw him. The season, focus and God questions fit exactly. It got thinner near the end: the 'say one thing' list and the 'what's behind the good' follow-up are built for hard seasons or spiritual moments, so a busy, fine, drifting person has to settle for 'Thank You.' and 'Everything, really'.

verdict.why: Line 1 describes Marcus's month almost word for word: "God has slipped into the background" is his own "background music" picture, and he would tap "Yes, that's it" straight away. Psalm 103 is a good fit for him. His life is busy but good, and "do not forget all His kind deeds" asks him to notice the good things he is already rushing past: the kids, the job, the hockey. It does not treat him as someone in crisis. Athanasius's advice, "stir up your own soul", reads like a nudge, not a scolding. One small snag is the second half of the line, "you want to wake your soul up to Him again". Marcus has drifted more than he has been wishing to come back, so that half reads a little aspirational, but he would accept it. Lines 1 and 3 both lead to Psalm 103. He would never see line 3, but it shows the ranking offers the same result twice. Line 2 ("empty and listless") would misread him because he is not worn down, and the ranking correctly puts it lower.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. "You want to wake your soul up" may give a faint guilty twinge about the reading plan he dropped, but the psalm answers that with blessing, not reproach.
verdict.theirSituation: A busy, good season in which God has quietly faded into the background; he has drifted more than he has actively longed to come back.

results.desc: Priya, 24, London, UK, raised Baptist. She started her first proper job in marketing and moved into a flat share in Walthamstow six weeks ago. She's mostly excited but lonely at weekends and hasn't found a church she likes yet. She talks to God on the bus but it feels thinner than it used to.

answers.wanted: Settling in somewhere new: making friends and finding a church. 'People in my life' sounded like trouble with people I already know, not a lack of people.
'My old friends are far away, and the new people are nice but I don't really know them yet.' 'Far away, or gone' sounds like someone died.
'Thinner than it used to be.' I still talk to Him but it feels faint. 'Drifted' felt too strong and 'background' makes it sound like I don't care.
Something like 'Help me find my people here' or 'Don't let me lose You in all this change.' 'I miss You' is near but sounds more dramatic than I feel.

'A fresh start: a new job, a new city.' 'A new home, or a new family' fits the flat, but 'new family' made me pause, and most of the other options are about God doing something specific, which I couldn't honestly say.

friction.note: There is no option for loneliness or finding community or a church. 'People in my life' reads as conflict or drama, so a lonely person who has just moved has nowhere obvious to tap.

'Far away, or gone' lumps friends who live in another city together with bereavement or estrangement. It felt heavy for 'my mates are in another town'. The question also assumes the people around you are doing something to you; 'I don't really have people here yet' is missing.

The list jumps from 'drifted' to 'background' to 'near, but quiet'. The very common feeling that prayer is still there but faint or thinner is missing. 'I've drifted from Him' also carries a faint note of blame.

Fourteen options is a lot to scroll on a phone. Most are cries of crisis ('How long?', 'Clear my name.', 'It isn't fair.'), and for someone in an up-and-down but basically OK season they feel over the top.

'What's behind the good?' assumes I'd put my season down as good; I said 'Up and down' and 'Lonely'. Most options point to God doing something visible ('I can see Him leading me', 'An answered prayer', 'Coming back to Him'), which feels a bit like being nudged to give a spiritual answer. There is no option for a plain fresh start: a new job or a new city.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly easy. The season, trend and feelings questions fitted me well, but a lonely new-in-town person with no conflict and no crisis kept landing on 'close enough', and the later questions leaned towards trouble with people or visible answers from God.

verdict.why: Line 1 describes her closely: faith that "feels thinner than it used to" and a wish to feel it again is what she's living. She'd tap "Yes" on the first line. Psalm 103 fits someone who is mostly excited about a new job and flat. "Bless the LORD, O my soul... do not forget all His kind deeds" gives her something to say on the bus, and it turns her real gratitude (the job, the move) into a way back in. It won't make her feel boxed in. What's missing is her loneliness at weekends and not having a church yet. Psalm 103 speaks to neither. Line 2 almost catches the church search, but "the home with Him that lasts forever" steers it toward heaven, which isn't her. So the result helps but only partly sees her.
verdict.wouldHurt: "Slipped into the background" is a little stronger than her reality: she still talks to God every day, it just feels thin. She might flinch slightly, as if she were being told she had drifted. Nothing wounds, though.
verdict.theirSituation: She's six weeks into a new city and job, mostly happy but lonely at weekends and without a church, and her prayer life still goes on but feels thin.

results.desc: Lucas, 15, São Paulo, Brazil, Catholic. He goes to confirmation classes on Saturdays because his mum wants him to, and school weeks are the same every week. He isn't sure he believes all of it, but he's not upset about that either. Mostly he's bored and thinking about football and a girl in his class.

answers.wanted: Bored
Football, and a girl I like (something like 'Someone I like' or 'Fun stuff / my hobbies')
Nothing really / 'Are You even real?' said casually, not as a cry. Something like 'Not much, honestly.'

friction.note: No 'Bored' option, which is the most common teenage state. The list leans heavy (afraid, ashamed, bitter, numb); for a kid who is just fine and bored it feels like the quiz expects something to be wrong.
'Someone I love' is too big a word for a crush, and 'People in my life' is vague. Nothing covers hobbies, sport or fun, which is what he actually thinks about.

Every option is an emotional prayer ('How long?', 'Stay with me.', 'Make me who You want me to be.'). For someone who isn't sure and isn't bothered about it, this reads as preachy and forces him to pick a feeling he doesn't have. 'Are You there?' sounds anguished rather than casually doubtful. A neutral option like 'Nothing, really' is missing.
'I'm not sure He's there' and 'Just there, in the background' are both close for him; the second fits better but a mild 'I don't think about Him much' would be clearer.
Fine. 'Quiet and ordinary' fitted exactly; though 'Same every week' might land better with a teen.

results.overall: Quick and easy for the first half, but a bored, lukewarm 15-year-old runs out of fitting options by the feelings and 'say one thing to Him' questions, which assume more emotional and spiritual intensity than he has. He'd finish it, but feel slightly boxed into sounding more troubled or devout than he is.

verdict.why: The first half, "God has slipped into the background", is exactly Lucas. He goes to confirmation because his mum wants him to, and his head is on football and a girl, not on God. The second half, "you want to wake your soul up to Him again", assumes a longing he doesn't really feel. He isn't looking to reconnect; he's just drifting and fine with it. Still, it's the only line that comes near, so he'd tap yes with a shrug. Line 2 is wrong: nothing is weighing on him. The fallback would be worse, because all three of its options are about suffering, and he isn't suffering. Psalm 103 is warm and not preachy, and "do not forget all His kind deeds" is a gentle nudge rather than a scolding. But to a bored 15-year-old, "Bless the LORD, O my soul" may read as more confirmation-class material instead of something about his own life.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. The only misread is "you want to" in line 1, which gives him a spiritual desire he doesn't have. It could feel slightly like being told what he should want, which is exactly how confirmation class feels.
verdict.theirSituation: He's a teenager going through the motions of faith out of habit and his mum's wishes: not upset or searching, just indifferent, with his mind on everyday life.

results.desc: Helen, 58, Cape Town, South Africa, Anglican. Nothing is wrong: her job is steady, her kids are grown, and her health is fine. But for about a year her prayers have felt like talking to the ceiling, and the services she used to love now feel flat. She keeps going and waits.

answers.wanted: Fine, but spiritually dry. Nothing's wrong, it just feels flat
Flat, or dry. Numb is too strong, but nothing else says 'the colour's gone out of it'
Silent, like talking to the ceiling. I'm not asking for anything to change, I just can't feel Him

friction.note: "Fine on the outside, not on the inside" sounds like hidden distress or depression. Helen isn't distressed, she's dry. It was the nearest option, but she'd worry it sends her down a 'something's wrong with you' path. She needs a quiet option like 'Fine, but flat inside' or 'Spiritually dry'.
None of the 17 words means flat or dry, which is the most common way people describe this season. Numb overstates it. 'Flat' or 'Dry' would be an honest tap.

"Silent. I pray and nothing changes" suggests she's praying for an outcome that isn't coming. Her prayers aren't petitions. They just seem to go nowhere. The first half ('Silent') fits and the second half pushes her toward an unanswered-request story. 'Far away' was also close, so she hesitated between the two.
This one worked well. 'I miss You.' is exactly her. 'Are You there?' was a close second, but it could read as doubting He exists, which she doesn't.

results.overall: Quick and mostly painless. The last question landed well. But a woman in an ordinary dry spell, with nothing wrong in her life, had to put herself one notch more troubled than she is on three questions ('not on the inside', 'Numb', 'nothing changes'), because none of them offers 'dry' or 'flat'.

verdict.why: Line 1 misreads me. I haven't nearly slipped or lost my footing. I keep going to church and I keep praying, and I'm waiting. "Honest enough to admit it" sounds like a confession I don't owe. Line 2 is the first one I'd say yes to. As written, "God's house" and "the home with Him that lasts forever" point toward heaven, and I'm not longing for heaven. But the verse underneath is me: "my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God." I miss the God I used to feel in those courts. So I'd tap yes, but because of the verse, not the line. Line 3 is wrong. Life hasn't worn me down. My job, my children and my health are all fine, and that's what makes this so strange. Nothing in the quiz names the thing itself: God feeling silent, prayer going nowhere, worship gone flat while life is good. The psalm that fits me best is actually Psalm 42 ("Where is your God?", "Hope in God, for I shall yet praise Him"). It only appears in the fallback, behind "weighing on me", and that framing suggests a heaviness I don't really feel.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing hurts. Line 1 would put me off a little if I read it as an accusation that my faith is slipping, when my faithfulness through the flatness is the one thing I'm holding onto. Line 2's heaven wording could read as "you're tired of this life", which isn't me.
verdict.theirSituation: Life is steady and nothing is wrong, but for a year God has felt silent and worship has felt flat. She keeps showing up and waits, missing His presence rather than being crushed or tempted.

results.desc: Paolo, 33, Manila, Philippines, Catholic. He's been offered a job in Dubai that would pay three times what he earns now, but it would mean leaving his wife and toddler for two years. He has a week to decide. He keeps asking God for a clear sign and hasn't got one.

answers.wanted: At a crossroads: a big decision in front of me
I have a big choice to make, soon
A big decision (money vs. being with my family); money and 'someone I love' both pull at me too, and I'd have picked two if allowed
Quiet when I need an answer. I keep asking for a sign and get none. It's not that 'nothing changes', it's that nothing is being said
Nothing good is behind it, or I can't tell yet. It's an offer I have to decide on, not a blessing. Maybe 'I don't know if it's good yet'

friction.note: Picking 'Something new is starting' dropped me into 'What's behind the good?', as if anything new has to be good. For me the new thing is a painful choice. The question tells me how I should feel about it, and I had to force an answer.
Nothing fits a person facing a decision. My life isn't hard or good, it's at a fork. A 'Big decision ahead' option would have caught me right away.
'Something new is starting' is vague. Is it the job offer, or the move that hasn't happened yet? A decision still ahead isn't really something that has started.
Only one pick, but my problem sits across three options: money, what's next, and the people I love (wife and child). Having to choose one feels like a box.
'I pray and nothing changes' fits someone waiting on a situation to change. I'm waiting for guidance. 'Silent' is right, the second half isn't.

results.overall: The questions were quick and mostly easy for Paolo, and 'Anxious, Unsure' and 'Show me the way.' fit him exactly. The quiz has no place for someone standing at a decision, though, and the follow-up treated his hard choice as a good thing to be thankful for.

verdict.why: Line 1 is close, since he is uneasy and it won't settle. But "downcast" and "weighed down" describe sadness, and Paolo isn't sad. He is torn and waiting for guidance, so he would tap "Not quite." Line 2 describes exactly where he is: he can't decide alone, and he keeps bringing it to God. Psalm 143:8, "Teach me the way I should walk, for to You I lift up my soul," is almost word for word the prayer he has been praying all week. The "morning" in that verse also fits a man counting down to a deadline. 143:10, "May Your good Spirit lead me on level ground," gives him something steadier than the sign he keeps asking for. As a Catholic he would find the psalm and the Father natural. He would feel seen and would want to screenshot 143:8.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. The only weak spot is Athanasius's advice line, "you have Psalms 5 and 143." Next to a verse that fits him this well, it reads flat and like a catalogue entry. A line about asking God to show the way, in the Father's own words, would land better.
verdict.theirSituation: A husband and father who has a week to decide whether to leave his family for two years for a much better-paid job abroad, and who keeps asking God for a clear sign without getting one.

results.desc: Fiona, 45, Glasgow, Scotland, nominally Church of Scotland. She goes to church at Christmas and for christenings. Lately she has been watching videos online arguing the Bible isn't reliable, and she's a bit unsettled by them, though not distressed. She wonders if there's anyone actually there, and would quite like there to be.

answers.wanted: Whether any of it is true, or whether there's anyone there. I don't really have a 'faith' as such.

friction.note: "God, and my faith" assumes I have a faith to think about. I'm a Christmas-and-christenings person who's been watching videos saying the Bible isn't reliable. Something like "God, and whether it's all true" would fit me without making me feel I'm claiming more than I have.

"And God, right now, feels..." starts from the idea that He's there. "I'm not sure He's there" saves it, but it sits in the middle of a list where most options assume a relationship with Him (drifted, displeased, close, clearly at work). It could put off a doubter for a second. Nothing in it is about the Bible itself, which is the actual thing unsettling me.

Talking to Him with a capital Y 'You' feels a bit like praying when I'm not sure I believe. Still, "Are You there?" is exactly what I'd say, so it works. Most of the other options ("Make me who You want me to be", "How great You are") would feel like church words to me.
No problem here. 'Unsure' and 'Curious' fitted well, and I liked not being pushed toward 'Hopeful' or 'At peace'.

results.overall: Quick and mostly painless. The questions let a doubter answer honestly, and 'Are You there?' landed. A couple of spots assume I already have a faith, and nothing touches my real question, whether the Bible can be trusted, so I'd be curious but a bit wary about which psalm it gives me.

verdict.why: As Fiona, line 1 is the only one near me. My doubts about whether anyone is there feel like a wobble in my footing, so I'd tap "Yes" with a little hesitation. "Come close to losing your footing" is a bit stronger than I feel, since I'm unsettled, not falling apart. "Honest enough to admit it" flatters me a touch. Psalm 73 does speak to me: verse 2 names the wobble, and verse 23 ("Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand") is exactly the answer I'd like to be true when I wonder if anyone is there. Line 2 is clearly not me, because I'm not marvelling at anything right now. None of the fallback options fit either: nothing is grinding me down, weighing on me or making me afraid.
verdict.wouldHurt: It doesn't wound, but it partly misreads me. Most of Psalm 73 is about envying wicked people who prosper, and my doubt is intellectual: videos saying the Bible isn't reliable. Reading the whole psalm, I might think "this isn't my problem" until verse 23. The Athanasius line is ungrammatical and confusing ("whatever in you has slipped comes to admit it"), which undercuts trust just when I'm doubting sources. The psalm also assumes I'm already speaking to God, which I'm not sure I can do. That is gentle, but nothing on the page names doubt about whether God exists.
verdict.theirSituation: A lapsed, nominal churchgoer who is quietly unsettled by online arguments against the Bible's reliability and wonders, without distress, whether God is really there, hoping He is.

results.desc: Gary, 62, St Paul, Minnesota, Lutheran. He retires from the county roads department at the end of next month. He's pleased and has plans for the lake cabin, but he keeps wondering who he'll be without the job and how he'll fill a Tuesday. He's thankful to God, if a little restless.

answers.wanted: Good, but a big change is coming (retiring next month)
Something new is about to start. It hasn't started yet, it's next month
Near, and I'm thankful, but I don't think about it every day
Thank You, and show me what to do with myself next. He'd have wanted to pick two here
A long job finished well, and retirement coming. None of the options is about work ending or a new stage of life

friction.note: The options (new home or family, coming to faith, coming back to Him, answered prayer) all assume a religious or family event. There's nothing for 'a career wrapping up' or 'a new stage of life', so a retiree is pushed onto 'Everything, really', which isn't true either. 'Coming to faith' and 'coming back to Him' sound churchy to a Lutheran who never left.
Nothing covers 'good but about to change a lot'. 'Good' leaves out the restlessness and 'Up and down' overstates it.
'Something new is starting' is close, but for him it hasn't started yet. He'd hesitate over whether a change coming next month counts.

Only one pick is allowed, but a thankful but restless person wants both 'Thank You.' and 'Show me the way.' Having to choose feels like a box. 'Make me who You want me to be.' is close to his worry about who he'll be without the job, but it sounds a bit like church language.
A steady churchgoer who isn't in crisis finds it hard to choose between 'Just there, in the background' (which sounds like a confession of neglect) and 'Close' (which feels like overclaiming).

results.overall: The core questions were quick and mostly fitted, and the 'Restless' and 'What's next for me' options named his situation well. The quiz kept treating a good but unsettled life change (retirement) as either plainly good or a spiritual event, and the follow-up about the good had nothing that fitted him.

verdict.why: As Gary I'd tap "Not quite" on the first line. I'm restless, but I'm not weighed down or downcast. "Won't settle" catches a bit of the Tuesday worry. "Weighed down" makes a good season sound like a heavy one, and I wouldn't say that about myself. The second line I'd take right away. I am thankful to God for a long job and a good ending to it, so "Yes, that's it." Psalm 103 fits a man retiring better than the quiz probably knows. "Who satisfies your years with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle" speaks to a new chapter. "Do not forget all His kind deeds" is a good way to look back over forty years of work. The line says nothing about the part of me that wonders who I'll be without the job. The psalm touches it gently through "as for man, his days are like grass" and "the LORD's loving devotion is from everlasting to everlasting." So the result speaks to me even though the prompt only named the thankful half.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds. The one small misread is that the first line shown, "weighed down or uneasy," was the best match for my answers. That tells me my restless answers got read as distress, and it would feel a bit off to see that at the top.
verdict.theirSituation: A thankful man about to retire, looking forward to it, a little restless about who he'll be and how he'll fill his days once the job ends.

results.desc: Mei Lin, 28, Singapore, baptised in an evangelical church six months ago. She and her boyfriend of two years broke up last month; it was mutual and probably right, but the evenings feel empty. She's a bit flat rather than heartbroken. Her faith is new, and she's not sure whether God cares about something this ordinary.

answers.wanted: Kind of flat and empty
Flat (numb is too strong, but nothing else says 'meh and empty')
Someone I was close to isn't around anymore
I don't know if He cares about something this small
Do You care about this?

friction.note: There's no low-key 'a bit flat' option. 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside' sounds more dramatic than how she feels, and 'Quiet and ordinary' makes it sound like nothing's wrong. She ends up on a stronger option than she'd like.

The mild words are all positive (Calm, Hopeful). On the low side everything is strong (Sad, Numb, Hurt), so there's nothing for being flat or empty without being really sad. 'Numb' reads as clinical to her.
'Far away, or gone' could mean someone died. For an ex after a mutual breakup, 'gone' feels too heavy. A plainer option like 'Someone close isn't in my life now' would fit better.

The options assume a settled faith with a history ('I've drifted from Him', 'Displeased with me'). A six-month believer's real question is whether God cares about ordinary things, and nothing says that. 'Displeased with me' could make a new believer wonder whether she should feel that.

Most options are strong laments ('How long?', 'Clear my name.', 'It isn't fair.'). For a mild, ordinary sadness they feel melodramatic. It's also hard to pick just one, and nothing asks whether He cares. 'Stay with me.' was the closest.
'Someone or something I've lost' is close, but a mutual breakup doesn't quite feel like a loss. She hesitated between that and 'People in my life'.

results.overall: The quiz was quick and easy to tap through on a phone, and no follow-ups came up. But nearly every question pushed her toward something heavier than she feels. The quiz seems built for big crises and not for a quiet, ordinary low patch. The god and say questions also left her real question unasked: does God care about something this small?

verdict.why: Line 1 almost gets her, because "empty and listless" describes her evenings exactly. But "life has worn you down" and "you need comfort" describe a long, grinding exhaustion, and she would feel she was claiming more suffering than she has. The breakup was mutual and a month ago. She is flat, not crushed. Psalm 102's "withered like grass; I even forget to eat my bread" would read as melodramatic for her, so she taps "Not quite". Line 2 is softer, and "something in you is weighed down or uneasy, and it won't settle" fits the restless, low evenings well enough. "Why are you downcast, O my soul?" is the right size for her: gently low, not devastated. Psalm 42 also answers her real, unspoken question of whether God cares about something this ordinary. The psalmist talks to his own soul and says "Put your hope in God". That is a new believer's prayer and needs no great crisis to earn it. She would feel quietly seen, not boxed in. The one gap: nothing names the loneliness or the empty space where a person used to be. So it lands as "near enough", not "that's exactly me".
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing in Psalm 42 would hurt her. The only risk is that the full psalm's "my tears have been my food day and night" and "deep calls to deep... all Your waves have gone over me" run heavier than her mood, which could make her feel she is being dramatic. The turn back to "Put your hope in God" steadies that. Had she stopped at line 1, Psalm 102 (withered, not eating, "like a pelican of the wilderness") would have overstated her state. It would also have deepened her worry that God only cares about big suffering.
verdict.theirSituation: A new Christian, a month past a mutual breakup, who feels flat and lonely in the evenings rather than heartbroken, and who wonders whether God cares about a sadness this ordinary.

results.desc: Jorge, 41, Lima, Peru, evangelical. The car needed a new gearbox and school fees are due, so he's working overtime and has put some of it on a card. It's manageable but it sits in the back of his mind. He trusts God will provide, mostly, and prays about it on the drive to work.

answers.wanted: Somewhere between 'Hard, but I'm getting by' and 'Busy, but fine'. Something like 'Stretched thin, but managing'.
Something like 'I trust Him, mostly' or 'Faithful. I'm waiting on Him'. It isn't that God feels quiet. He's leaning on Him and waiting to see the provision.
'Provide for us' or 'I'm trusting You with this'. 'Help.' sounds more desperate than he feels, and 'Show me the way' is about guidance, not provision.

friction.note: 'Hard, but I'm getting by' and 'Busy, but fine' both half-fit someone who is under strain but coping. He'd hesitate between them, and 'hard' may sound more dramatic than his situation.
None of the fourteen lines says trust or asks God to provide ('Give us what we need' / 'I trust You'), even though that is the most common prayer about money. 'Help.' alone reads like a crisis.
No option for steady but slightly strained trust. 'Near, but quiet' suggests God is silent, which isn't quite how he'd put it.

results.overall: Quick and easy. Money, 'Worn out' and 'Anxious' felt spot on. But the quiz leans toward either crisis or bliss, so an ordinary 'stretched but trusting God' week had to be pushed into 'Hard' and 'Help.'. No follow-ups came up, so it felt short.

verdict.why: Line 1 is too heavy. I'm stretched, not empty or listless, and saying yes would mean admitting a despair I don't feel. Line 2 misses too: I'm not living afraid, and I do already take heart in God, mostly. Line 3 is the nearest. I pray about this every morning on the drive, asking God to provide, so "you need to plead with God, and want words to pray with" fits closely enough to tap yes. It still says nothing about money or providing for the family, which is my actual situation. Psalm 5's morning verse (5:3, "In the morning... I lay my plea before You and wait in expectation") would genuinely land, since that is exactly my drive to work. But most of Psalm 5 is about liars, the wicked and enemies. That has nothing to do with a gearbox and school fees, so reading it in full I'd feel the psalm answers a different problem. It's a verse to hold onto, not a psalm about my life right now. A line about trusting God to provide, or worry that sits in the back of the mind, would have fit far better, but the letter apparently doesn't name one.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. The only jar is that the rest of Psalm 5 is about enemies and deceitful men, which could make me feel the quiz took my money worry for a conflict with people. The 988 crisis line would not fit here either (it's also a US number and I'm in Peru), but on this path it probably would not show.
verdict.theirSituation: A steady believer praying through ongoing but manageable money pressure (car repair, school fees, some card debt). He isn't in despair or fear. He wants a psalm about trusting God to provide while carrying a low-level worry.

results.desc: Karen, 50, Wichita, Kansas, Southern Baptist. Her 14-year-old golden retriever is slowing down, and the vet says it may be weeks rather than months. Otherwise life is ordinary: work, church on Sunday, her husband's knee surgery recovery. She feels a bit silly being this sad about a dog and hasn't prayed about it.

answers.wanted: Mostly ordinary, but one thing has me sad
I just got some sad news I'm waiting on (the vet's weeks, not months)
My dog, or a pet I love. I paused between 'Someone I love' and 'Someone or something I've lost', because he's not gone yet and he's not a 'someone'
I haven't really said anything to Him about it. Maybe 'Help me let him go'

friction.note: Nothing covers a pet. 'Someone I love' and 'Someone or something I've lost' both sort of fit, but neither is right: the dog is still alive, and 'someone' makes her feel sillier for counting a dog. A line like 'someone I love, person or pet', or an option for a loss that's coming, would help.

There's nothing between 'Quiet and ordinary' and 'Fine on the outside, not on the inside'. That second one sounds like a hidden crisis, which is too dramatic for being sad about an old dog, so she picks 'ordinary' and plays her sadness down.

'Something hard just happened' doesn't really fit news about a loss that hasn't happened yet. 'Getting worse' sounds like her whole life is going downhill. There's no option for a hard thing she can see coming.

The question assumes she's been talking to God about it, and she hasn't. There's no gentle choice like 'I haven't said anything yet'. The prayer-shaped options make her feel a bit guilty for not praying.
'I'm losing them' fits well, but 'them' reads oddly for a dog. It isn't a problem, just a small reminder that the quiz was written with people in mind.

results.overall: It was quick and mostly easy. The sad-and-losing path matched her by the end. But she had to squeeze a pet into questions written about people, and play her sadness down as 'quiet and ordinary'. That quietly confirmed her feeling that this grief doesn't really count.

verdict.why: As Karen, I'd say yes to the first line. I am weighed down, and it isn't lifting. It's quiet, dull sadness more than restlessness, but the line is close enough to take. It also doesn't make me name the dog or explain why I'm sad, and that's a relief because I feel silly about it. "Why are you downcast, O my soul? Put your hope in God" fits someone who hasn't prayed about this yet. It takes my sadness seriously without calling it too small. It also gives me words to start praying with, which is exactly what I haven't done. As a Southern Baptist I know Psalm 42, and seeing it chosen for me would feel like permission to grieve. Lines 2 and 3 wouldn't fit, because God hasn't slipped away from me and I'm not pleading for anything. The fallback's "It's weighing on me" would also have led to Psalm 42, so the quiz would have reached the same psalm either way.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounding. Two parts of the full psalm wouldn't fit her. The first is the taunting enemies of 42:3 and 42:10 ("Where is your God?"): no one is mocking her. The second is the psalmist's longing to go back to the house of God, and she is in church every Sunday. Neither would hurt her. They would just read as not about her, while the refrain speaks straight to her.
verdict.theirSituation: Karen is quietly grieving ahead of time for an old dog who is dying, feels embarrassed that it hurts this much, and hasn't brought it to God, so she is sad more than uneasy.

results.desc: Dawit, 20, Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, Ethiopian Orthodox. He's in the middle of exams and mostly goes to liturgy because his mother expects him to. His cousin is getting baptised next month and has asked him to stand with him, which made him think about how far he has drifted. He isn't unhappy, just not very present to God.

answers.wanted: Exams make it the same as always, but the cousin's baptism is a small nudge. Something like 'Something is making me think' would fit better.
Distracted, or a bit guilty. Not ashamed, just aware that he has let things slide.
Something between 'I'm sorry' and 'I miss You', like 'I haven't been showing up.' 'I'm sorry' sounds heavier than he feels.
'Not showing up, just letting it slide' or 'Going through the motions.' He hasn't done anything. It's neglect, and every option assumes a specific wrong or a struggle.

friction.note: Every option assumes a real wrongdoing, a relapse or a warning from God. Someone who tapped 'I'm sorry' because he drifted gets pushed into calling it a 'habit' or 'something I did'. It needs a quiet option like 'Just letting it slide' or 'Going through the motions'.
'A sense that God is warning me' feels heavy and a little alarming to a young man who is only lukewarm.
Nothing fits 'fine but disconnected': no 'distracted', 'guilty' or 'going through the motions'. 'Unsure' and 'numb' are the nearest, and both overstate it.
'I'm sorry' is the only apologetic option, and it sends him down the sin path. A drifting person who isn't in distress may feel boxed in by that tone.
Nothing covers 'something small made me stop and think' (the cousin asking him to stand with him). That was the real prompt for his reflection, and the quiz never catches it.
There's no way to say 'people expect things of me' (his mother and liturgy), which is a big part of his situation, though 'Fine' covers it well enough.

results.overall: Quick and mostly easy. The drift option on the God question felt spot on and made him feel seen. After that the path treated his lukewarmness like a sin to confess, and the 'Which is closest?' follow-up forced him to pick an answer he didn't believe.

verdict.why: Line 1 isn't me. I haven't done some particular wrong that I'm ashamed of and want to confess. I've drifted: I go to liturgy because my mother expects it, and I'm busy with exams. Saying yes to "you're ashamed" would be claiming a guilt I don't feel, so it's "Not quite". Line 2 is also off. I'm tired from exams but I'm not worn down, empty or needing comfort, and I'm not unhappy. Line 3 is exactly me. God has slipped into the background, and my cousin asking me to stand with him at his baptism made me want to wake up to Him again. Psalm 103 fits because it isn't a psalm of crisis or shame. "Bless the LORD, O my soul... do not forget all His kind deeds" is a man talking to his own sleepy soul, and that's what I need. I could pray it before liturgy or on the day of the baptism. Athanasius's note is about thanksgiving more than drift, but "stir up your own soul" bridges the gap well enough. One snag: my church uses the Greek (Septuagint) psalm numbers, where this psalm is 102. If I looked it up in my own Psalter (Mezmure Dawit) I'd open the wrong psalm, and the next line down on the list, Psalm 102, would add to the confusion.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing wounds me. Two things could misread me. If the list stopped at line 1, it would suggest drifting means I'm living in unconfessed shame, and that would feel like being told off. Also, the psalm numbers follow the Hebrew count with no Greek number beside them, so an Orthodox reader using his own Psalter would open Psalm 103 in his Psalter (Psalm 104 in the Hebrew count), not this one.
verdict.theirSituation: A young Ethiopian Orthodox man who isn't in crisis or ashamed, just drifting and half-present at liturgy, and his cousin's coming baptism has made him want to wake up to God again.

results.desc: Aoife, 31, Dublin, Ireland, Catholic. Her daughter is eight weeks old, she is exhausted, and she is happier than she has ever been. Her father, who she hadn't spoken to in three years, came to the christening and they talked for an hour afterwards. She keeps saying thank you to God in the middle of night feeds.

answers.wanted: Really good, but I'm wrecked. Happiest I've ever been and more tired than I've ever been.
Something new is starting AND something hard is finally over (me and my dad). I can only pick one.
Grateful, Happy and Worn out. All three are true and I had to drop Happy.
A new baby / my family growing, and my dad coming back into my life

friction.note: Single choice means the reconciliation with her father (a rift that has ended) disappears once she picks 'Something new is starting'. The 'over' and 'rift' follow-ups she'd have loved are never reached. Let her pick two here, or ask about any ended rift some other way.
No option for 'exhausted but joyful'. New parents, carers and people in a demanding but good season all hit this. 'Really good' leaves out the tiredness and 'Up and down' gets the mood wrong.
The two-pick cap hurts when the honest answer is a mix, like grateful plus happy plus worn out. She'd notice she had to leave out a positive word to admit she's tired.

'A new home, or a new family' reads like moving house or getting married. A new baby only just fits. Something like 'A new baby, or someone new in the family' would land. There's also no option for a relationship being mended, which is half of what's behind her good season.
'They're new in my life' is a slightly odd way to describe your own newborn, but she'd get it.

results.overall: Quick and mostly warm. The God, people and 'Thank You' questions fitted her perfectly. She'd feel a bit boxed in by single or two-pick answers, because her season is joy and exhaustion together, and the healed rift with her dad, which matters a lot to her, had nowhere to go.

verdict.why: Line 1 is exactly what I'm doing: saying thank you to God at 3am during feeds, for everything at once. I'd tap "Yes, that's it" without hesitating. Psalm 103 fits well. "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds" is what I keep whispering. It also has "as a father has compassion on his children" (103:13), which lands hard in a week when I've become a mother and got my own father back. Athanasius's "through everything and in everything" also covers the tiredness, which I liked. Line 3 was close too, because something new has started in our home. But "dedicate your house" sounds like getting a priest to bless a new flat, and Psalm 30 opening with foes rejoicing doesn't fit a happy christening. Line 2 was the only one that read me wrong: I'm exhausted but not empty, and I'd have been a bit put out if that had come first.
verdict.theirSituation: A new mother who is worn out but overflowing with gratitude, for her baby and for making peace with her father.

results.desc: Derek, 47, Houston, Texas, non-denominational. He picked up his five-year sobriety chip last Tuesday, and his teenage son came to the meeting to watch. Work is steady and he's paying off old debts one by one. He feels like God has been holding him up the whole time, even the years he didn't notice.

answers.wanted: Something to mark a milestone: 'I just hit a milestone' or 'Something I worked for is paying off.' 'Something hard is finally over' is tempting, but in recovery it's never over, so he wouldn't claim that.

'Staying on track / my recovery.' Really it's sobriety, his son, and paying off debts all at once. 'Money' and 'Someone I love' each cover only part of it, so he'd settle on God as the thread running through them.

'He carried me through,' or 'He held me up, even when I didn't notice.' He'd want an option about looking back and seeing he was held, not about God leading him forward. 'I'm growing' and 'His kindness' come near too.

friction.note: None of the options fits a milestone or an anniversary. For someone in recovery, 'Something hard is finally over' feels risky to tap because it isn't over, and 'Getting better' undersells a five-year chip.

No option covers recovery, a habit he beat, or rebuilding his life. 'Something I've done' reads as current guilt, not past wreckage he is repairing, so he'd steer away from it even though it's part of his story.

'What's behind the good?' only looks forward or at the present (leading, growing, answered prayer). The gratitude of looking back ('He held me up the whole time') has no clear option. 'Coming back to Him' is close, but he isn't sure he ever fully left.

results.overall: For Derek it was quick and mostly easy: the grateful, God-is-at-work answers were right there and felt natural. The one gap he'd notice is that nothing speaks to a recovery milestone or to looking back and seeing he was carried, so two or three taps were "close enough" rather than exactly him.

verdict.why: Derek's whole state right now is gratitude that looks back over everything, including the bad years. "Thank God, in and through everything" describes that closely. The "through everything" part fits his sense that God held him up even when he didn't notice. Psalm 103 is almost uncomfortably right for a man in recovery who is paying off old debts: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all His benefits". It goes on to God forgiving all our iniquities, redeeming our life from the pit, and not dealing with us according to our sins. He would feel seen, not boxed in. He would say yes to the first line straight away and never see the Psalm 23 line, though that one would have fit him nearly as well.

results.desc: Annamma, 73, Kottayam, Kerala, India, Mar Thoma Church. Her son, out of work for eight months, got a good job in Bangalore last week, which she had prayed for every morning. Her granddaughter's wedding is in December and the house is full of plans. She feels God has been kind to her family this year.

answers.wanted: Both 'Getting better' and 'Something hard is finally over' fit (eight months of my son without work just ended). I tapped the simpler one. What I'd really want to say is 'God answered my prayer.'
'My family': my son's new job and my granddaughter's wedding. 'Someone I love' is only one person, and 'People in my life' sounds like neighbours and friends.
'An answered prayer' is the main one, but I'd also tap 'His kindness, to me and to everyone'. It's my whole family's year, not one prayer. I'd have liked to pick two here.

friction.note: There's no 'My family' option. For an Indian grandmother the family is the whole picture, and she has to squeeze it into 'Someone I love' (just one person) or 'People in my life' (sounds like outsiders).
'Getting better' and 'Something hard is finally over' overlap when a long hardship has just ended. She may not know which to tap and may worry she picked wrong.

'What's behind the good?' is a slightly odd, abstract phrase for an older reader whose first language isn't English. 'What has made it good?' or 'Why has it been good?' would read more easily. Only one tap is allowed, but blessings usually come in more than one form.
Idioms like 'getting by', and on other screens 'turned on me' and 'drags', may not land for someone who speaks Indian English as a second language. Not a problem for her path, but worth noting.
'What's happening with them?' followed by 'They're doing well, and I'm thankful' fits. But it treats the loved one as a single case, and she has two happy events (the job and the wedding).

results.overall: It felt warm and easy for her. Most taps matched her grateful mood, and 'Thank You.' and 'Clearly at work' said exactly what she feels. The only snag was the lack of a 'my family' answer, plus two places where she wanted to tap two things (why she is thankful, and whether things are getting better or a hardship is over).

verdict.why: Annamma would say "Yes, that's it" to the first line. She mainly wants to thank God right now, and Psalm 103 fits her mood well. Its "do not forget all His kind deeds" matches a year of answered morning prayers for her son. The psalm also speaks of good things that satisfy and of mercy on children's children, which suits a wedding being planned. Line 2 might fit her a little more closely, since it is about God's kindness to "you". But line 1 comes first and is true enough that she would never reach line 2. One small snag: "in and through everything" sounds like thanking God in spite of trouble. Her gratitude is simpler: a specific prayer was answered.
verdict.wouldHurt: Nothing would wound her. At 73, the psalm's line about our days being like grass might make her pause, but it is gentle and she would know it well from church. Her church says the psalms regularly, so the result would feel familiar and fitting, not strange.
verdict.theirSituation: She is thankful because God answered a prayer she said every morning: her son got a job. Her family is also happily busy planning her granddaughter's wedding.

results.desc: Kwame, 26, Accra, Ghana, Methodist. He was promoted to team lead at the telecoms company and got engaged to Efua in the same month. He's grateful, a bit nervous about managing people older than him, and wants to stay humble about it. God feels close and generous right now.

answers.wanted: Grateful, and a bit nervous. 'Anxious' is stronger than what I feel. It's more jitters about a new responsibility.
Work and Efua both, pretty much equally. I'd have tapped two here if I could.
Thank You, and keep me humble. I'd want 'Thank You' and 'Make me who You want me to be' together.
A new job and a new family at once, and I can see God's hand in both. 'A new home, or a new family' only covers the engagement, so 'Everything, really' felt a bit vague.

friction.note: Nothing sits between 'Anxious' and 'Unsure' for being a little nervous about something good, like new responsibility. 'Anxious' makes a happy season sound heavier than it is.
Only one answer is allowed, but good seasons often have two things going on at once (a promotion and an engagement). Being forced to pick one feels like a box.

There's no option for asking God to keep me humble or to help me carry new responsibility well. 'Make me who You want me to be' is close but reads like a struggle or a confession. Allowing one or two picks, as the feel question does, would fix it.

'A new home, or a new family' fits the engagement but not the promotion, and 'I'm growing' sounds like personal growth, not a new role. 'Everything, really' is the catch-all but it feels generic. There's no option for a blessing that brings new responsibility.
Nothing picks up that the nerves come from managing people older than me. A happy person with some nerves may feel the quiz only hears the gratitude.

results.overall: It felt quick and friendly, and most of the questions fit a good season without pushing me toward sadness. My main wish was to tap two answers on 'focus' and 'say', and for a way to say 'grateful but a little nervous about the responsibility, keep me humble'. That was the heart of where I am.

verdict.why: Line 1 misses me. I am a little nervous about leading people older than me, but I am not "tired of living afraid", and saying yes to that would inflate a small worry into fear. Line 2, "thank God in and through everything", is exactly my month: the promotion and the engagement to Efua together, and God feels close and generous. Psalm 103:2, "do not forget all His kind deeds", names what I want to hold on to. The psalm also helps with staying humble: later on it says our days are like grass and that He knows we are dust, which speaks to the nerves about the new role without calling them fear. I would feel seen, not boxed in. One small thing: Athanasius pairs 103 and 104, so the result should print both or say why it shows only one. And "in and through everything" leans towards thanking God in hard times, when my situation is simply joy. It still fits.
verdict.theirSituation: A season of double blessing (promotion and engagement), grateful and wanting to stay humble, with only a slight nervousness about leading older colleagues.

results.desc: Margaret, 80, a village in Devon, UK, Church of England. Her days are quiet: the garden, the Wednesday coffee morning, phone calls with her grandchildren. Her hip aches but her health is good for her age. She feels God near in a calm, unhurried way and is content.

answers.wanted: My grandchildren. 'Someone I love' is singular, and she has several. 'People in my life' felt too vague, and her hip is only a small niggle.

Something like 'The small, everyday blessings', meaning the garden, coffee mornings and phone calls. 'How good and well-made everything is' nearly fit because of the garden, but it sounds grander than how she feels.

friction.note: 'This stretch of your life' reads like it was written for someone in the middle of a phase or a busy period. At 80, her whole retirement is one long steady stretch. 'Quiet and ordinary' is exactly right, though.

Every option except 'Nothing in particular' assumes something is on her mind or bothering her. There is nothing for someone content, whose mind is on small good things like the garden. 'Someone I love' is singular, which fits the grandchildren only loosely. 'Work or school' is irrelevant to her, but that's harmless.

Most of the fourteen options are distress cries ('How long?', 'Why?', 'I'm so tired.'). A contented person has to read through a list of anguish before reaching 'Thank You.' It's a long list to scroll on a phone.

'What's behind the good?' is slightly odd, clipped phrasing. Several options ('A new home, or a new family', 'Coming to faith', 'Coming back to Him', 'I'm growing') assume a recent change or event, and an unchanging, long-settled contentment has no clear home besides 'Everything, really'.
Fine overall. A Church of England reader might hesitate between 'Near, but quiet' and 'Close', but that's a fair distinction, not a problem.

results.overall: It felt pleasant and quick, and she was never pushed toward a crisis answer. But the quiz clearly expects someone who is going through something, so a contented, settled person keeps finding that the most specific options are about trouble or change, while her own kind of quiet everyday gratitude has only general options.

verdict.why: Margaret is quietly content and feels God near, so "You want to thank God, in and through everything" describes her. It is a gentle line and it doesn't box her in. Psalm 103, "Bless the LORD, O my soul... do not forget all His kind deeds", is one she would know well: the Church of England hymn "Praise, my soul, the King of heaven" is based on it. At 80, with a sore hip but a good life, remembering God's benefits is where she is, and Athanasius's advice to stir up your own soul to bless Him would feel like a warm, fitting word. She would feel seen. One risk in the draft: this was the only line offered. If it had missed, the fallback assumes something is wrong ("grinding me down", "weighing on me", "afraid"), which doesn't fit a contented person at all. A calm or grateful person needs a second or third line, such as praise, trust or evening peace, before the quiz falls back to hardship.

results.desc: Andrei, 35, Bucharest, Romania, Romanian Orthodox. He and his older brother had not spoken for six years over their father's inheritance, and at Easter they finally sat down and made peace. Last Sunday he stood as godfather when his best friend was baptised as an adult. He feels lighter than he has in years.

answers.wanted: Both at once: the six-year feud with my brother is finally over, and something new is starting (I just became a godfather). Picked the ending because it is the bigger thing.
My brother and my best friend, the people I love. I wavered between 'People in my life' and 'Someone I love', because it is two people and both are good news.

friction.note: I can only pick one, but my life has an ending and a new start at the same moment. Because I chose 'finally over', the quiz never asked about the good part (the baptism, the new godson), so half of why I feel lighter never came in.

Never asked. My answers were Really good, Grateful, and 'finally over', and that did not unlock 'What's behind the good?', even though its options 'Coming to faith, someone else's' and 'A new family' fit me exactly. It feels like the quiz only looks at the ending and not at the joy.

'We made peace' is right, but it is the only option without God in it. Every other option is 'He answered' or 'He got me out'. I made peace with my brother at Pascha, and for me that was God's doing too, so I wanted an option that said both, like 'We made peace, and God was in it'.
'A falling-out' is too small a word for six years of silence over our father's inheritance. It sounds like a quarrel. 'A long rift in my family' would fit better.
'People in my life' and 'Someone I love' overlap for me. It was not clear which one to pick when the person on my mind is my brother.

results.overall: Quick and mostly natural. The questions let me say that things are good and grateful without sounding pious. The one frustration was that choosing 'finally over' seemed to shut out the joyful half of my story, the baptism and becoming a godfather, so the result may catch the reconciliation but miss the new beginning.

verdict.why: Andrei is overflowing with gratitude: six years of silence with his brother are over, and he just stood as godfather at his friend's baptism. "You want to thank God" is true of him, and "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all His kind deeds" is what he would want to say, so he taps yes. The phrase "in and through everything" is a little broad for him. He isn't thanking God through hardship right now. He's thanking God for two particular mercies, and neither of them, the brother or the baptism, is named. It lands as good but generic, not as "this is exactly me". If Athanasius's letter has a line pairing the harmony of brothers with Psalm 133 ("how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity"), it would speak to him far more directly and should be checked for. For an Orthodox reader, Psalm 103 (102 in his Septuagint numbering) is familiar and loved, which helps. The fallback screen is built around suffering ("grinding me down", "afraid"), which would feel badly wrong to him, but he never reaches it.
verdict.theirSituation: He is grateful and at peace after making up with his brother, whom he hadn't spoken to in six years, and after becoming a godfather. So his thanks is for a reconciliation and a new spiritual bond, not general thanks "through everything".
